title: United Kingdom | Money Laundering Regulations 2017 and POCA Compliance
tagline: Know the UK rules cold: POCA offences, MLR due diligence, SARs and consent, OFSI sanctions and your bank's AML programme.
sectors: Payments and trade finance teams in UK banks
description:
A UK-specific anti-money laundering, counter-terrorist financing and counter-proliferation financing quest for bank staff. It is based on the **Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017** (as amended, including **SI 2026/621**), **Part 7 of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002**, the **Terrorism Act 2000** and UK financial sanctions made under the **Sanctions and Anti-Money Laundering Act 2018**, as supervised and enforced by the **FCA**, the **NCA's UK Financial Intelligence Unit** and **OFSI** (HM Treasury).

Regulation 24 of the MLRs requires banks to make relevant employees, and agents doing similar work, aware of the law on money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing and to train them regularly to recognise and deal with suspicious activity. This quest supports that duty for front-line, operations, compliance and management staff, and ends with real FCA enforcement cases.

It builds knowledge of the UK framework and does not replace your bank's own policies, procedures or role-specific training.
audience: Branch, contact-centre and relationship staff in UK banks who open accounts and handle payments
KYC, onboarding and EDD analysts applying the MLRs to individuals, companies and PEPs
Transaction monitoring, SAR and sanctions screening teams
Trade finance and payments operations staff exposed to sanctions and proliferation financing risk
MLROs, deputies and senior managers with responsibility for financial crime controls
outcomes: Explain the UK AML/CTF/CPF framework and the roles of the FCA, NCA UKFIU and OFSI
Identify the POCA and Terrorism Act offences, including failure to disclose and tipping off
Apply MLR risk assessment, CDD, EDD and proportionate PEP measures, including the 2026 amendments
Make internal reports and explain the SAR and DAML process and its statutory time limits
Handle sanctions screening hits, asset freezes and OFSI reporting, and recognise proliferation financing
Describe the bank's programme: nominated officer, regulation 24 training, record keeping and enforcement

cards.title: Day one: the jeweller's cash
cards.setting: Financial crime office, Larkhill Bank plc, Manchester. Monday, 8:50 am.

lines.text: Your new pass still has the plastic film on it when a video call pings onto the big screen in the MLRO's office.
Welcome to Larkhill. I'm Priya Raman, the bank's MLRO and nominated officer. Your quest starts now: by Friday you will know the UK rules well enough to defend them in front of the FCA.
Priya, it's Callum in Glasgow. A jewellery wholesaler has paid in GBP 48,000 in cash this week. Scottish and English notes, bundled with elastic bands, and the notes smell damp.
The owner says it's trade takings. My cashier has a bad feeling, but nobody has seen a crime. Do we have to do anything?
Amara Okafor, investigations. Callum, the law doesn't wait for proof. A suspicion is enough to trigger a duty for your team.
Exactly. So, new analyst: which UK laws are we under here, what offences are in play, and who must do what by when? That's Stage 1.

cards.title: The UK rulebook in five pieces

scenes.heading: POCA 2002, Part 7
scenes.narration: The Proceeds of Crime Act creates the money laundering offences and the duty for people in the regulated sector to report knowledge or suspicion. It is criminal law, and it applies to you personally.

scenes.heading: Terrorism Act 2000
scenes.narration: The Terrorism Act makes it an offence to raise, use, hold or arrange funds for terrorism, and gives bank staff a separate duty to disclose suspected terrorist financing.

scenes.heading: Money Laundering Regulations 2017
scenes.narration: The Regulations tell the bank how to run its defences: a written risk assessment, policies and controls, customer due diligence, a nominated officer, staff training and record keeping.

scenes.heading: Sanctions under SAMLA 2018
scenes.narration: Sanctions regulations made under the Sanctions and Anti-Money Laundering Act 2018 freeze the assets of designated persons. HM Treasury's Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation, OFSI, enforces the financial side.

scenes.heading: Who watches and who listens
scenes.narration: The FCA supervises banks for the Money Laundering Regulations and financial crime systems. The National Crime Agency's UK Financial Intelligence Unit receives suspicious activity reports. FATF sets the global standard the UK follows.

cards.title: Match the offence to the section
cards.prompt: Link each POCA or Terrorism Act section to what it makes an offence.

pairs.right: Concealing, disguising, converting, transferring or removing criminal property from the UK
Entering into or becoming concerned in an arrangement that you know or suspect helps someone else with criminal property
Acquiring, using or possessing criminal property
Failing to disclose knowledge or suspicion of laundering that came to you in regulated business
Revealing a disclosure or an investigation in a way likely to prejudice it
Arrangements that help someone keep or control terrorist property

cards.question: Under POCA, when is property 'criminal property'?
options: Only when a court has convicted someone of the crime that produced it
When it is, or represents, a benefit from criminal conduct and the person dealing with it knows or suspects that
Only when it comes from drug trafficking, terrorism or fraud above a set threshold
When the bank's monitoring system has generated an alert on it
cards.explanation: POCA defines criminal property by two elements: it represents a benefit from criminal conduct, and the person knows or suspects that. No conviction or minimum crime type is needed, and criminal conduct includes conduct abroad that would be an offence in the UK.

cards.title: Knowledge, suspicion and 'reasonable grounds'
cards.body:
The **principal offences** (ss.327 to 329) need the person to **know or suspect** that property is criminal. A bank employee who processes a payment they suspect is laundered can commit one.

The **regulated-sector reporting offence** (s.330) goes further. It is committed if you know or suspect, **or have reasonable grounds** to know or suspect, that someone is laundering, the information reached you at work, and you do not report it to the **nominated officer** (or the NCA) **as soon as practicable**. That is an objective test: ignoring obvious warning signs is no defence.

Two protections matter to you:
- An **authorised disclosure** (s.338), made before you act and followed by **appropriate consent**, is a defence to the principal offences.
- Under **s.330(7)**, a person who did not actually suspect **and** was never given the training their employer should provide has a defence. That is one reason regulation 24 training matters so much.

cards.title: Which offence is in play?
cards.prompt: Sort each situation by the POCA offence it most closely risks.

items.text: A clerk knowingly moves suspected fraud proceeds into a customer's offshore account
An adviser helps a client set up a loan he suspects will hide drug money
An employee buys a car cheaply from a customer she suspects is selling stolen goods
A cashier notices repeated damp cash bundles and odd stories but tells nobody
A relationship manager ignores obvious warning signs and makes no internal report
A teller tells a customer 'we've reported you, so watch what you pay in'
A manager warns a friend that the bank's investigators are looking at his account

cards.title: Callum's doubt
cards.setting: Video call, Glasgow branch and Manchester. 10:15 am.

lines.text: But if we report him and he's honest, can he sue us? And what if I'm wrong?
A disclosure made in good faith under POCA does not breach confidentiality, and the Act protects you from civil liability for it. You don't need to be right. You need to be honest and prompt.
And remember who you report to. Staff report internally to me as nominated officer. I decide whether a SAR goes to the NCA.
So my cashier's job is to tell you, not to investigate or confront him.
Spot on. Let's test that instinct.

cards.title: The cashier's choice
cards.situation: Your Glasgow cashier, Ewan, is serving the jewellery wholesaler again. Another GBP 9,500 in damp, rubber-banded notes. The customer jokes: 'Busy week, don't ask!' Ewan's training says unusual cash patterns are a warning sign. The deposit is small enough to process normally. What should Ewan do?

choices.text: Process the deposit, then make an internal report to the nominated officer as soon as practicable, following the bank's procedure
choices.outcome: Right. Ewan has reasonable grounds to suspect, so s.330 requires an internal report as soon as practicable. Priya can then consider whether the bank needs consent before dealing further. Ewan stays calm and says nothing to the customer.

choices.text: Refuse the deposit and tell the customer the bank suspects the cash is dirty
choices.outcome: Telling the customer what the bank suspects risks tipping him off and prejudicing an investigation. Ewan has also not reported anything, so the s.330 duty is still unmet.

choices.text: Call the local police directly and skip the bank's internal process
choices.outcome: A disclosure to a constable is lawful, but bypassing the nominated officer means the bank loses control of the case and may miss a consent decision for future transactions. Use the internal route unless told otherwise.

choices.text: Process it and say nothing: one deposit under GBP 10,000 is not his business
choices.outcome: There is no minimum amount for suspicion. Saying nothing when there are reasonable grounds to suspect risks the s.330 offence, which carries up to five years on indictment.

cards.title: Real case: NatWest's criminal conviction (2021)
cards.body:
In December 2021 **National Westminster Bank Plc** was fined about **GBP 264.8m** at Southwark Crown Court after pleading guilty to three offences of failing to comply with the Money Laundering Regulations 2007. It was the **first criminal prosecution the FCA brought** under the Regulations.

- The customer was **Fowler Oldfield**, a Bradford jewellery business. NatWest expected no cash, yet around **GBP 365m** was deposited, about **GBP 264m** of it in cash.
- Branch staff **did report suspicions** (Scottish notes paid in across England, musty-smelling notes, nervous couriers), but **no appropriate action followed**.
- The monitoring system **recorded some cash deposits as cheques**, hiding the risk.

**Lesson:** reporting is only half the system. Reports must be investigated, escalated and acted on. Source: FCA press release, 13 December 2021.

cards.front: Myth: you need proof of a crime before you report.
cards.back: Fact: suspicion, or reasonable grounds to suspect, is enough. Investigating is the job of the nominated officer and law enforcement.

cards.front: Myth: only cash can be criminal property.
cards.back: Fact: any property counts, including bank balances, cars, crypto and rights over assets, if it represents a benefit from crime.

cards.front: Myth: if the crime happened abroad, POCA doesn't apply.
cards.back: Fact: criminal conduct includes conduct abroad that would be an offence if it happened in the UK (with narrow exceptions).

cards.front: Myth: reporting to my line manager discharges my duty.
cards.back: Fact: the s.330 duty is met by disclosure to the nominated officer (or the NCA). Follow the bank's internal reporting route.
Fact: regulation 24 requires it, and s.330(7) links the reporting offence to whether your employer trained you.

cards.question: Ewan had no actual suspicion, but a trained colleague would have spotted obvious warning signs. Ewan has had the bank's regulation 24 training. Could he commit the s.330 offence?
options: No, because s.330 needs actual suspicion
Yes, because s.330 also covers reasonable grounds to know or suspect, and the training defence is not open to him
No, because only the nominated officer can commit s.330
Only if the amount exceeds the POCA threshold for banks
cards.explanation: Section 330 has an objective limb: reasonable grounds to know or suspect. The s.330(7) defence needs both no actual suspicion and no employer-provided training. Ewan was trained, so it does not help him.

cards.title: Real case: Santander UK (2022)
cards.body:
In December 2022 the FCA fined **Santander UK Plc** about **GBP 107.8m** for serious and persistent gaps in its AML controls over business banking between 2012 and 2017, affecting more than **560,000** business customers.

- Santander did not properly verify what customers said their business would do, or compare expected and actual deposits.
- One new 'translation business' expected about GBP 5,000 a month, yet received millions within six months and moved the money on quickly.
- The AML team recommended closure in March 2014, but it was not acted on until September 2015.
- In total more than **GBP 298m** passed through such accounts before closure.

**Lesson:** a sound decision is worthless if the bank's processes cannot carry it out. Source: FCA press release, 9 December 2022.
