cards.title: Stage 1 take-aways
items: POCA Part 7 and the Terrorism Act set criminal offences that apply to you personally; the MLRs set the bank's systems.
Criminal property is any benefit from crime that the person knows or suspects is criminal; no conviction or threshold is needed.
In the regulated sector you must report knowledge, suspicion or reasonable grounds to suspect to the nominated officer as soon as practicable.
An authorised disclosure plus appropriate consent is your defence to the principal offences.
The FCA supervises, the NCA's UKFIU receives SARs and OFSI enforces financial sanctions.

cards.prompt: Think of a payment, deposit or customer story you saw in the last month that felt slightly off. Under s.330's 'reasonable grounds' test, would a trained colleague have reported it? What would you write in your internal report?

quiz.question: A customer at a Leeds branch pays in GBP 6,000 in used notes and says it is a gift from an uncle. The cashier thinks the story is odd but cannot say why. Under POCA, what is the cashier's legal position?
options: No duty arises unless the cashier can identify the specific crime that produced the cash and can point to evidence that the customer was involved in it
A duty arises only if the amount is GBP 10,000 or more in a single transaction
An internal report to the nominated officer is required as soon as practicable if the cashier suspects, or has reasonable grounds to suspect, laundering
The cashier should ask the customer for proof of the uncle's income before deciding anything
quiz.explanation: Section 330 is triggered by knowledge, suspicion or reasonable grounds to suspect; no specific crime or threshold is needed. Asking for proof is not wrong in itself, but it does not replace the duty to report a suspicion.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the difference between POCA Part 7 and the Money Laundering Regulations 2017?
options: POCA applies only to banks while the MLRs apply to all individuals
The MLRs create the money laundering offences that individuals can commit, while POCA sets out the training, record keeping and risk assessment duties for firms
POCA is FCA guidance while the MLRs are an Act of Parliament
POCA sets criminal offences; the MLRs require firms to run systems such as risk assessment, CDD, training and records
quiz.explanation: POCA Part 7 is criminal law: ss.327-329 offences, s.330 failure to disclose and tipping off. The MLRs are regulations setting the systems firms must operate. The training duty sits in MLR regulation 24, not POCA.

quiz.question: A relationship manager agrees to route a customer's 'consultancy fees' through a new account even though she suspects they are bribes. Which POCA offence is she most at risk of?
options: Section 333A, tipping off
Section 330 only, because she works in the regulated sector
Section 328, being concerned in an arrangement she suspects helps another person use or control criminal property
No offence, because bribery is dealt with by the Bribery Act 2010 rather than POCA, so the bribes are not criminal property for laundering purposes
quiz.explanation: Facilitating another person's control or use of suspected criminal property is the s.328 arrangements offence. Bribes are criminal property under POCA. She also has a s.330 duty, but the arrangement itself risks the principal offence.

quiz.question: Under POCA s.338, what makes a disclosure 'authorised' so that it can give a defence to the principal offences?
options: It is made to the customer's solicitor before the transaction is processed
It is made to a constable, customs officer or nominated officer, normally before the prohibited act is done
It is made in writing to the FCA's financial crime department within 30 days of the transaction, with copies of the customer's identification documents
It is made to any manager at the bank after the transaction completes
quiz.explanation: Section 338 lists the recipients (constable, customs officer, nominated officer) and timing conditions, mainly disclosure before the act. The FCA and line managers are not the statutory recipients, and no 30-day rule exists.

quiz.question: An employee did not suspect anything about a customer, but a reasonable trained employee would have. The bank never gave her any AML training. Which is correct?
options: She may have a defence under s.330(7): she did not suspect and her employer never gave her the specified training
She has no defence, because the objective 'reasonable grounds' test always applies to anyone working in the regulated sector, whatever training they received
Only the bank can be liable, because individuals cannot commit s.330
She is protected only if she later made a report to the NCA
quiz.explanation: Section 330(7) gives a defence where the person did not know or suspect and the employer did not provide the specified training. It shows why regulation 24 training protects both staff and the bank's control framework.

quiz.question: Who receives suspicious activity reports (SARs) from UK banks?
options: The UK Financial Intelligence Unit within the National Crime Agency
The FCA's enforcement division
OFSI at HM Treasury
The Prudential Regulation Authority
quiz.explanation: SARs go to the NCA's UK Financial Intelligence Unit. The FCA supervises AML systems, OFSI deals with sanctions reports and the PRA is the prudential regulator.

quiz.question: A customer's funds came from tax evasion committed in another country where that conduct is also a crime. The bank's staff suspect this. Does POCA's definition of criminal conduct cover it?
options: Yes, criminal conduct includes conduct abroad that would be an offence if it occurred in any part of the UK
No, POCA only covers crimes committed in England and Wales
Only if the foreign country has already convicted the customer
Only if the funds exceed the threshold amount that POCA sets for banks operating accounts, because smaller overseas amounts fall outside UK law
quiz.explanation: Under s.340, criminal conduct covers conduct that is, or would be if it occurred in the UK, an offence. Overseas conduct is caught, subject to narrow exceptions where it was lawful locally and not of a prescribed kind.

quiz.question: In the NatWest prosecution (2021), what did the FCA highlight as a key system failure?
options: The bank had no nominated officer at all during the period
The monitoring system treated some cash deposits as cheques, so high-risk cash activity was not properly monitored
Branch staff never raised any internal reports about the customer, so the bank's investigators had no way of knowing about the cash deposits
The bank refused to cooperate and was convicted after a full trial
quiz.explanation: The FCA said staff did report red flags but no appropriate action followed, and cash deposits were recorded as cheques. NatWest pleaded guilty; it did not go to a full trial.

quiz.question: Which authority enforces UK financial sanctions, including licences and breach penalties?
options: The NCA's UK Financial Intelligence Unit
The FCA's supervision division
The Information Commissioner's Office
OFSI, the Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation within HM Treasury
quiz.explanation: OFSI, part of HM Treasury, implements and enforces financial sanctions made under SAMLA 2018. The NCA handles SARs; the FCA supervises systems and controls, including sanctions controls, but OFSI handles licences and sanctions breaches.

quiz.question: A Birmingham teller is unsure whether a transaction is suspicious enough to report. What is the best course under the bank's POCA framework?
options: Wait for a second unusual transaction so the suspicion is stronger
Make the internal report and let the nominated officer, who has wider information, decide whether a SAR is needed
Ask the customer to explain the transaction in writing and only report it if the written explanation is unconvincing or inconsistent with the account history
Discuss the case with colleagues at lunch to see whether they share the concern
quiz.explanation: The nominated officer is there to weigh internal reports against all available information. Waiting or seeking written explanations can delay a report that must be made as soon as practicable, and chatting about it widely raises tipping-off and confidentiality risks.

sessions.title: Risk-Based Approach, CDD, EDD and PEPs under the MLRs
sessions.summary: Use the firm-wide risk assessment to drive customer due diligence, beneficial ownership checks, enhanced due diligence and proportionate treatment of UK and foreign PEPs.
objectives: Describe the regulation 18, 18A and 19 risk assessment and control duties
Apply CDD triggers and measures, including the sterling thresholds from June 2026
Decide when regulation 33 requires EDD and what regulation 31 requires when CDD fails
Treat domestic and non-domestic PEPs proportionately under regulation 35

cards.title: Two files, one deadline
cards.setting: Business banking floor, Larkhill Bank, London. Tuesday, 9:30 am.

lines.text: Morning! Two big wins for us. A property developer, Redcastle Holdings, wants a GBP 3m facility. And the husband of a sitting MP wants a mortgage. I'd like both signed off by Thursday.
Redcastle is owned through a holding company in another country, and then a trust. Do we know who really owns and controls it?
The director gave us a structure chart. Isn't that enough?
A chart is a claim, not verification. And the MP's husband is a family member of a PEP, so enhanced due diligence applies.
We can't treat a British MP's family like a foreign dictator!
You're half right, Tom. The law now says a domestic PEP starts from a lower risk. Stage 2 is about getting that balance right, using our risk assessment.

scenes.heading: Know your own risks first
scenes.narration: Regulation 18 requires the bank to identify and assess its money laundering and terrorist financing risks, looking at customers, countries, products, transactions and delivery channels. Regulation 18A adds proliferation financing.

scenes.heading: Write it down and keep it current
scenes.narration: The assessment must be recorded in writing, kept up to date, and given to the FCA on request. It must reflect the size and nature of the business.

scenes.heading: Build controls to match
scenes.narration: Regulation 19 requires policies, controls and procedures that manage those risks, approved by senior management, regularly reviewed and communicated to staff.

scenes.heading: Apply customer due diligence
scenes.narration: Part 3 of the Regulations sets out customer due diligence: when it applies, what it involves, and when it must be enhanced.

scenes.heading: Scale up and down
scenes.narration: Higher risk means enhanced measures. Lower risk can mean simplified measures where the Regulations allow it. The risk assessment is what justifies the choice.

cards.title: The UK risk-based approach as a loop
cards.caption: Each turn of the loop should use what monitoring, SARs and FCA feedback taught the bank.

items.label: Assess firm-wide risk
items.detail: Reg 18 and 18A: customers, countries, products, transactions, channels.

items.label: Set policies and controls
items.detail: Reg 19: proportionate, approved by senior management.

items.label: Apply CDD and monitoring
items.detail: Part 3: identify, verify, understand, monitor.

items.label: Review and update
items.detail: Keep records of changes and of how staff were told.

cards.title: CDD for a company customer
cards.prompt: Put the CDD steps for Redcastle Holdings in a sensible order.
steps: Obtain and verify the company's name, registration number and registered office
Establish the law it is subject to, its constitution and its directors and senior persons
Take reasonable measures to understand the ownership and control structure
Identify the beneficial owners and take reasonable measures to verify who they are
Assess and, where appropriate, obtain information on the purpose and intended nature of the relationship
Rate the risk and decide whether enhanced due diligence is needed
Monitor the relationship and keep the CDD information up to date

cards.question: Since 30 June 2026, when must a bank apply CDD to an occasional transaction (not a funds transfer) under regulation 27?
options: When it amounts to GBP 12,000 or more, in one operation or several that appear linked
When it exceeds EUR 15,000, converted at the day's rate
Only when it is paid in cash
Never, because banks only need CDD for business relationships
cards.explanation: SI 2026/621 replaced the euro amounts in regulation 27 with sterling ones from 30 June 2026: GBP 12,000 or more for occasional transactions, and over GBP 800 for an occasional transfer of funds. CDD also applies whenever there is suspicion or doubt about earlier ID.

cards.title: When CDD cannot be completed, and when you can rely on others
cards.body:
**Regulation 31.** If the bank cannot apply the CDD that regulation 28 requires, it must:
- not carry out transactions through a bank account with or for the customer;
- not open the relationship or carry out other transactions;
- end any existing relationship; and
- consider whether a disclosure is needed under POCA or the Terrorism Act.

Money deposited can be repaid to the person who paid it in, but if a disclosure is required the bank first needs the appropriate consent.

**Regulation 39 (reliance).** The bank may rely on another regulated firm (or an equivalent overseas firm) to carry out CDD, but it **remains liable** for any failure. It must obtain the CDD information straight away and have an agreement to get copies of the documents immediately on request. Reliance on a firm established in a FATF call-for-action country is not allowed.

cards.title: Is EDD required?
cards.prompt: Sort each case: does regulation 33 require enhanced due diligence, or may standard CDD be enough on these facts?

items.text: A new customer resident in a country on the FATF call-for-action list
The husband of a serving UK MP
A payment correspondent relationship with a bank outside the UK
A customer who gave a false passport, and the bank still wants to continue
A transaction unusually large for its nature, with no clear purpose
A salaried nurse in Leeds opening a current account, with nothing unusual
A UK company listed on a regulated market opening a deposit account
A local bakery whose owner and turnover match its records

cards.title: Domestic PEP or foreign PEP?
cards.caption: Regulation 35 as amended from 10 January 2024; FCA guidance FG25/3 explains proportionate treatment.

items.label: Starting point
items.left: Lower risk than a non-domestic PEP
items.right: Assessed on its own risk factors

items.label: EDD extent
items.left: Less, if no enhanced risk factors
items.right: Full EDD scaled to the risk

lines.text: So I need senior management sign-off for a mortgage to an MP's husband? That's red tape.

It's regulation 35. Approval, adequate measures on source of wealth and funds, and enhanced monitoring. But proportionate: for a UK PEP with no extra risk factors, light-touch EDD is the right answer.
The FCA's review found firms over-treating UK PEPs and their families, and staff training needing work. Refusing them out of fear is also a failure.
Fine. And Redcastle?
Overseas holding company, a trust, a big facility and a sector with laundering risk. That one gets the full treatment.

cards.title: The MP's husband
cards.situation: Daniel Hughes, husband of a serving UK MP, applies for a GBP 450,000 mortgage on a family home. He is a salaried engineer, the deposit comes from the sale of the couple's previous home, and there are no adverse media or other risk factors. Tom asks how the bank should handle it.

choices.text: Apply proportionate EDD: senior management approval, adequate checks on source of wealth and funds, enhanced monitoring, starting from a lower risk
choices.outcome: Correct. Regulation 35 requires these measures for a PEP family member, and since January 2024 a domestic PEP starts from a lower risk, so the EDD can be light where no other risk factors exist.

choices.text: Decline the application: PEP relationships are too risky for a retail bank
choices.outcome: Blanket refusal is not what the law requires. The FCA has criticised firms for disproportionate treatment of UK PEPs and their families. The bank should manage the risk, not avoid it.

choices.text: Treat him as a standard customer, because UK PEPs are now outside the EDD rules
choices.outcome: UK PEPs and their families still need EDD. The change lowered the starting point for the risk assessment; it did not remove senior management approval, source of wealth checks or enhanced monitoring.

choices.text: Apply the bank's heaviest EDD, demand ten years of tax returns, and review monthly
choices.outcome: This meets the letter of the law but ignores the lower starting point for domestic PEPs. It is disproportionate, slows a low-risk customer and wastes analyst time.

cards.title: Real case: Monzo (2025)
cards.body:
In July 2025 the FCA fined **Monzo Bank Ltd** about **GBP 21.1m** for weak financial crime controls between October 2018 and August 2020.

- Monzo grew from about 600,000 customers in 2018 to more than 5.8 million in 2022, but its controls did not keep pace.
- Onboarding, customer risk assessment and transaction monitoring were not adequately designed or run.
- Customers were onboarded on limited and sometimes **obviously implausible information**, such as well-known London landmarks given as home addresses.
- Under a requirement not to open accounts for high-risk customers, Monzo still signed up **more than 34,000** of them between 2020 and 2022.

**Lesson:** CDD is not a form-filling exercise. Fast growth needs controls that grow with it. Source: FCA press release, 8 July 2025.

cards.title: Real case: Barclays and WealthTek (2025)
cards.body:
In July 2025 the FCA fined Barclays a total of **GBP 42m** in two cases. In the first, **Barclays Bank UK PLC** (fined about **GBP 3.1m**) opened a client money account for **WealthTek** without gathering enough information to understand the money laundering risk.

- A simple check of the **FCA's Financial Services Register** would have shown WealthTek was **not permitted to hold client money**.
- Clients went on to deposit **GBP 34m** into the account.
- Barclays agreed to make a voluntary payment of about **GBP 6.3m** to affected clients.

**Lesson:** understanding the purpose and intended nature of the relationship includes checking that what the customer says it does is lawful and authorised. Source: FCA press release, 16 July 2025.

cards.back: Any individual who ultimately owns or controls more than 25% of shares or voting rights, or who otherwise controls the company or its management.
Only after exhausting all possible means may the bank treat the senior managing official as beneficial owner, and it must keep written records of what it tried.
Ownership-structure and beneficial owner steps do not apply to a company listed on a regulated market.
If the bank finds a material discrepancy with the Companies House register, regulation 30A requires it to be reported.
Scrutinise transactions against what you know of the customer, and keep CDD documents and information up to date (reg 28(11)).

cards.front: Source of wealth vs source of funds
cards.back: Wealth: how the person built their overall assets. Funds: where the money for this specific transaction comes from.

cards.question: Under regulation 35 as amended in 2024, what is the starting point when assessing a UK (domestic) PEP?
options: The same risk as a non-domestic PEP, with full EDD in every case
A lower level of risk than a non-domestic PEP, with less extensive EDD if no enhanced risk factors are present
No PEP measures at all, because the rules now apply only to foreign PEPs
A higher risk than a non-domestic PEP, because UK officials control UK budgets
cards.explanation: Regulation 35(3A) sets a lower starting point for domestic PEPs and their family members and known close associates, and less EDD where no enhanced risk factors exist. Approval, source of wealth and funds checks and enhanced monitoring still apply.

cards.title: Choosing the right level of CDD
cards.caption: Top row: higher product risk. Right column: higher customer risk. Your bank's risk assessment sets the actual rules.

items.label: Standard CDD
items.detail: Ordinary customer, ordinary product, clear purpose.

items.label: Targeted EDD
items.detail: Ordinary customer but a higher-risk product or channel, such as large cross-border flows.

items.label: Simplified CDD (where allowed)
items.detail: Low risk on all factors and the Regulations permit simplified measures.

items.label: Full EDD and approval
items.detail: High-risk customer and high-risk country or product, e.g. complex offshore ownership.

cards.title: Stage 2 take-aways
items: The bank must assess its ML, TF and PF risks in writing (regs 18 and 18A) and build senior-management-approved controls on them (regs 19 and 19A).
CDD means identify, verify, understand ownership and purpose, and keep monitoring; triggers include relationships, GBP 12,000 occasional transactions and suspicion.
If CDD cannot be completed, do not transact, end the relationship and consider a disclosure (reg 31).
Regulation 33 lists EDD cases, including FATF call-for-action countries, PEPs, correspondent relationships and unusual transactions.
UK PEPs still need EDD, but start from a lower risk; reliance never moves liability away from the bank.

cards.prompt: Pick one customer type you deal with. Using the five risk-factor areas (customers, countries, products, transactions, channels), how would you rate it, and what single piece of information would most change that rating?

quiz.question: Redcastle Holdings is owned 60% by an overseas holding company, which in turn is owned by a trust. The director has supplied a structure chart. What must Larkhill do about beneficial ownership?
options: Understand the ownership and control structure, then identify the individuals behind it and take reasonable measures to verify them
Accept the director's chart, because the director signs a declaration of truth
Record the overseas holding company as the beneficial owner, since it holds more than 25% of the shares and is itself a regulated entity in its home country
Refuse the customer, because trusts cannot be beneficial owners under the MLRs
quiz.explanation: Regulation 28 requires the bank to understand the ownership and control structure and to identify and take reasonable measures to verify beneficial owners, who are individuals. A company cannot be the end of the chain, and a declaration alone is not verification.

quiz.question: Which of these must the bank's firm-wide risk assessment under regulation 18 take into account?
options: Only the countries on the FATF call-for-action list
Only the risks identified in the most recent FCA visit
Only customers already rated high risk
Risk factors relating to customers, countries or areas, products or services, transactions and delivery channels
quiz.explanation: Regulation 18(2) lists five risk-factor areas and information from the supervisor. A narrower view, such as only high-risk customers or only FATF-listed countries, would not meet the requirement.

quiz.question: A customer cannot provide verification of her identity and the bank cannot complete CDD. She asks the bank to transfer her account balance to a third party. What does regulation 31 require?
options: Make the transfer to the third party as instructed, then close the account within 30 days and record that CDD could not be completed
Transfer the funds as long as the third party is a UK bank account
Freeze the account and report the customer to OFSI
Do not make the transfer; end the relationship and consider whether a POCA or Terrorism Act disclosure is needed
quiz.explanation: Regulation 31 prohibits transactions through a bank account where CDD cannot be applied, requires termination and requires the bank to consider a disclosure. Funds may only be repaid to the person who deposited them, with consent if a disclosure is needed. OFSI deals with sanctions, not CDD failures.

quiz.question: Larkhill relies on another UK-regulated bank to carry out CDD on a shared corporate client. Later, the other bank's CDD proves defective. Who is liable under regulation 39?
options: Only the bank that carried out the CDD
Larkhill remains liable for any failure to apply the CDD measures it relied on
Neither, if the reliance agreement was in writing
Liability is shared equally by statute
quiz.explanation: Regulation 39(1) allows reliance but states that the relying firm remains liable. Reliance saves effort; it does not transfer responsibility.

quiz.question: Which customer requires enhanced due diligence under regulation 33 as amended by SI 2026/621?
options: Any customer resident in a country that is not a member of FATF or of one of the FATF-style regional bodies
Any customer who makes an international payment
A business customer incorporated in a country on FATF's call-for-action list
Any company that does not have a UK director
quiz.explanation: From 30 June 2026 the regulation 33 country trigger is a FATF call-for-action country, replacing the earlier 'high-risk third country' test. Non-membership of FATF, foreign payments or foreign directors are risk factors to weigh, not automatic EDD triggers.

quiz.question: A Glasgow branch customer, the adult daughter of a serving UK MP, opens a savings account funded by her salary. There are no other risk factors. How should the bank approach her?
options: As a domestic PEP family member: EDD from a lower starting point, lighter where no enhanced risk factors exist
As a non-domestic PEP family member, because she lives in Scotland rather than Westminster, so full EDD and senior management approval are required
As a standard customer, because adult children are never PEP family members
As a prohibited customer until her parent leaves office
quiz.explanation: Children of a PEP are family members under regulation 35, and an MP is entrusted with prominent public functions by the UK, so she is a domestic PEP family member. The lower starting point applies, and with no other risk factors the EDD can be light. PEP status is never a reason to refuse outright.

quiz.question: A former UK minister left office eight months ago. Can the bank stop applying PEP measures now?
options: No. The measures continue for at least 12 months after leaving office, or longer if the bank judges it necessary
Yes, PEP status ends on the day the person leaves office, so the bank can move the customer to standard CDD straight away and stop enhanced monitoring
Yes, but only for domestic PEPs
No, PEP measures continue for life
quiz.explanation: Regulation 35(9) requires the measures to continue for at least 12 months after the person ceased to hold the prominent public function, and for longer where the bank considers it appropriate. They do not end immediately, nor last automatically for life.

quiz.question: In the Monzo case (2025), what onboarding weakness did the FCA highlight?
options: Monzo refused to open accounts for any customers without a UK passport
Customers were onboarded on limited, sometimes obviously implausible information, such as well-known landmarks as home addresses
Monzo relied entirely on other banks' customer due diligence under regulation 39 and never checked the documents it received from them
Monzo onboarded no high-risk customers during the period
quiz.explanation: The FCA said Monzo onboarded customers on limited and implausible information, and signed up more than 34,000 high-risk customers despite a requirement not to. The case is about weak onboarding and risk assessment, not reliance.

quiz.question: Barclays Bank UK PLC opened a client money account for WealthTek in the case the FCA decided in 2025. What simple check did the FCA say would have revealed the risk?
options: A check of the UK Sanctions List, which would have shown that WealthTek's principal partner was a designated person at the time
A search of the FCA's Financial Services Register, which showed WealthTek was not permitted to hold client money
A Companies House search, which showed WealthTek had been dissolved
A credit reference check on WealthTek's principal
quiz.explanation: The FCA said looking at the Financial Services Register would have shown WealthTek was not permitted to hold client money. The case is about understanding the nature and purpose of the relationship, not sanctions or credit risk.

quiz.question: The bank's onboarding team finds that Companies House lists a different person with significant control from the one the bank has verified as beneficial owner. What should happen?
options: Ignore it, because Companies House data is not the bank's responsibility
Update the bank's records to match Companies House without further enquiry
Investigate, and if it is a material discrepancy, report it as regulation 30A requires
Close the account immediately and file an OFSI report
quiz.explanation: Regulation 30A requires banks to report material discrepancies between what they find and the register. Copying the register blindly defeats the purpose of verification, and OFSI is not the right channel.

sessions.title: Suspicion, SARs, the DAML Regime and Tipping Off
sessions.summary: Follow a suspicion from the counter to the NCA: internal reports, the nominated officer's decision, consent requests and the statutory clock, without tipping anyone off.
objectives: Make a clear internal report to the nominated officer as soon as practicable
Explain the DAML notice period, moratorium and court extensions under POCA
Recognise and avoid tipping off under POCA s.333A and Terrorism Act s.21D
Apply the Terrorism Act disclosure duty for suspected terrorist financing

cards.title: The car dealer's payment
cards.setting: Investigations room, Larkhill Bank, Manchester. Wednesday, 8:40 am.

lines.text: Morning. Brightmoor Motors, a Leeds car dealer, has received forty payments from different private individuals in three weeks. Now it wants to send GBP 180,000 to a company abroad.
And Leeds raised an internal report yesterday. The director said the overseas firm is a 'parts supplier', but there are no invoices.
So I have an internal report and a payment waiting. If we send that money and it is criminal property, the bank could commit a principal offence.
Which means we may need a defence against money laundering from the NCA before we act.
At 9:02 the phone rings. The Brightmoor director wants to know why his payment hasn't gone.
Stage 3: suspicion, SARs, consent and the line you must never cross, tipping off. Let's work it through.

cards.title: From a hunch to the NCA

scenes.heading: Someone notices
scenes.narration: An employee sees something that gives them knowledge, suspicion or reasonable grounds to suspect laundering. They report it internally to the nominated officer as soon as practicable.

scenes.heading: The nominated officer decides
scenes.narration: Regulation 21 requires the nominated officer to weigh each internal report against everything the bank knows, and decide whether there is knowledge or suspicion.

scenes.heading: A SAR goes to the NCA
scenes.narration: If so, the nominated officer must disclose to the NCA's UK Financial Intelligence Unit as soon as practicable. Failing to do so is an offence under section 331.

scenes.heading: Consent before acting
scenes.narration: If the bank needs to do something with the suspected property, such as making a payment, it makes an authorised disclosure and asks for a defence against money laundering, often called a DAML.

scenes.heading: The statutory clock
scenes.narration: The NCA has seven working days to refuse. If it refuses, a 31-day moratorium starts, which a court can extend. When the time runs out without action, consent is treated as given.

cards.title: The DAML clock under POCA s.335 and s.336A
cards.caption: Working days exclude weekends, Christmas Day, Good Friday and bank holidays where the disclosure is made.

items.label: Authorised disclosure
items.detail: The nominated officer asks for consent to do the prohibited act, such as a payment.

items.label: Notice period
items.detail: Seven working days starting with the first working day after the disclosure.

items.label: No refusal received
items.detail: Consent is treated as given at the end of the notice period.

items.label: Refusal received
items.detail: A 31-day moratorium starts on the day notice of refusal is received.

items.label: Court extensions
items.detail: Each extension up to 31 days; no more than 186 days in total beyond the first 31.

items.label: Moratorium ends
items.detail: When the moratorium (as extended) expires, consent is treated as given.

cards.title: Who does what in a SAR case?
cards.prompt: Match each person or body to its role when Brightmoor's payment is held.

pairs.right: Reports suspicion to the nominated officer as soon as practicable
Considers the report with all available information and decides on a SAR or DAML request
Receives the SAR and the request, and may refuse consent within the notice period
May extend a moratorium on application by a senior officer
Must not pressure staff to release the payment or skip the process

cards.question: Priya submits a DAML request on a Thursday. When does the notice period run, assuming no bank holidays?
options: Seven calendar days from Thursday
Seven working days starting with Friday, the first working day after the disclosure
31 days from the date of the request
Until the NCA writes back, however long that takes
cards.explanation: Section 335(5) sets the notice period at seven working days starting with the first working day after the disclosure. The 31-day period is the moratorium that starts only if consent is refused.

cards.title: What a good internal report and SAR contain
cards.body:
Section 330(5) describes the **required disclosure**:
- the **identity** of the person suspected, if you know it;
- the **whereabouts of the laundered property**, as far as you know; and
- the **information** that gave you the knowledge or suspicion.

A useful internal report answers: **who** (customer, counterparties), **what** (amounts, products, accounts), **when** and **where**, and, most important, **why** it seems suspicious compared with what the bank knows about the customer.

Write facts, not accusations. You do not need to name a crime. Do not investigate further yourself, do not ask the customer leading questions about the report, and keep a note that you reported.

A **DAML request** must also say exactly **which act** the bank wants to do (for example, 'pay GBP 180,000 to account X'), so the NCA knows what it is consenting to.

cards.title: At the counter: from doubt to report
cards.prompt: Put Callum's team's actions in the right order when something feels wrong.
steps: Notice the unusual activity and compare it with what you know about the customer
Carry on serving the customer normally, without revealing any concern
Write down the facts: who, what, when, where and why it seems unusual
Submit an internal report to the nominated officer through the bank's system as soon as practicable
Follow the nominated officer's instructions on whether any transaction may proceed
Keep the report confidential and tell nobody outside the need-to-know chain

cards.title: The angry phone call
cards.setting: Leeds branch, back office. Wednesday, 9:05 am.

lines.text: The Brightmoor director is on the line to the Leeds branch manager, who has looped in Callum for advice.
He says: 'Have you lot reported me to the police? Just tell me straight, or I'm moving all my accounts today.'
Careful. If anyone reveals that a disclosure was made, or that an investigation is likely, and that is likely to prejudice it, that's tipping off under section 333A.
Our script says payments can be delayed by standard checks and we'll be in touch. Say nothing about reports, the NCA or police. Log the call and send it to me.
Calm, factual, and nothing about the report. Got it.

cards.title: Answering the Brightmoor director
cards.situation: The director of Brightmoor Motors demands to know why his GBP 180,000 payment has not been sent and whether the bank has 'reported him'. A DAML request is with the NCA. The Leeds manager must respond now.

choices.text: Explain that payments can be delayed while the bank completes its standard checks, promise an update, then log the call and pass it to the nominated officer
choices.outcome: Correct. This is truthful, does not reveal the disclosure or any investigation, and gives Priya useful information. Agree any wording with the nominated officer's team.

choices.text: Tell him honestly that the bank has asked the NCA for consent and must wait seven working days
choices.outcome: This reveals that a disclosure was made. If it is likely to prejudice an investigation, it is the s.333A tipping-off offence, which carries up to two years' imprisonment.

choices.text: Release the payment to calm him down and avoid a complaint
choices.outcome: Making the payment before consent or the end of the notice period could be a principal offence under s.327 or s.328 for the bank and the staff involved.

choices.text: Refuse to discuss anything and end the call
choices.outcome: This avoids tipping off but damages the relationship and may itself raise suspicion. A calm, scripted response is better. Partly right.

cards.front: What are the two s.333A offences?
cards.back: Revealing that a disclosure (SAR) was made, or that an investigation is being contemplated or carried out, where that is likely to prejudice an investigation.

cards.front: Does it apply only to the person who made the SAR?
cards.back: No. Anyone who learned the information in regulated-sector business can commit it, including colleagues who were told.
Up to two years' imprisonment on indictment, a fine, or both.

cards.front: Can banks ever share SAR information?
cards.back: Yes, but only within the permitted disclosures in ss.333B to 333D, such as within a group or between institutions in limited cases. Follow the MLRO's instructions.

cards.front: Is asking normal CDD questions tipping off?
cards.back: No. The offence is about revealing a disclosure or an investigation. Routine questions about a transaction are part of good due diligence.
Section 21D of the Terrorism Act 2000 creates a parallel tipping-off offence for the regulated sector.

cards.title: Escalate or explain?
cards.prompt: Sort each observation: should it go to the nominated officer, or is it ordinary activity to note and continue?

items.text: Many small payments from unrelated individuals into a business account, quickly sent abroad
A customer who asks how much cash can be paid in before 'forms are filled in'
Funds moved on the same day they arrive, with no business reason given
A customer insisting a payment be split just under the bank's review amount
A retailer's card takings rising in December, in line with previous years
A salaried customer's monthly mortgage payment going out on payday
A small business paying its regular suppliers listed in its CDD file

cards.title: Real case: Barclays and Stunt & Co (2025)
cards.body:
In July 2025 the FCA fined **Barclays Bank PLC** about **GBP 39.3m** for failing to manage money laundering risk in its relationship with **Stunt & Co**.

- Barclays did not gather enough information at the start or carry out proper ongoing monitoring.
- In just over a year, Stunt & Co received **GBP 46.8m** from **Fowler Oldfield**, the money laundering operation at the centre of the NatWest case.
- Barclays did not properly consider the risk **even after receiving information from law enforcement** and after learning that police had raided both firms.
- It reviewed its exposure only after learning that the FCA would prosecute NatWest.

**Lesson:** a warning from law enforcement is a trigger to re-assess the whole relationship at once, not to wait. Source: FCA press release, 16 July 2025.

cards.title: From alerts to intelligence
cards.caption: Each layer narrows the volume, but every layer must be documented.

items.label: Monitoring alerts and staff concerns
items.detail: Automated alerts and front-line observations.

items.label: Internal reports
items.detail: Concerns that give knowledge, suspicion or reasonable grounds to suspect.

items.label: Nominated officer review
items.detail: Weighed against everything the bank knows.

items.label: SARs to the NCA
items.detail: Disclosures where suspicion is confirmed.

items.label: DAML requests
items.detail: Where the bank needs consent to do a prohibited act.

cards.question: A cashier at Larkhill tells a colleague in another branch that 'Priya has SAR'd the Brightmoor guy'. The colleague happens to know the director and warns him. Who may have committed tipping off?
options: Nobody, because the cashier only told a colleague
Only the cashier, because he started the chain
The colleague who warned the director, if it was likely to prejudice an investigation, and the cashier's gossip is a serious breach of confidentiality
Only Priya, as the nominated officer responsible for the SAR
cards.explanation: Section 333A is committed by whoever discloses the matter in a way likely to prejudice an investigation, using information gained in regulated business. The colleague warned the subject. The cashier's chat outside the need-to-know chain breaks bank policy and created the risk.

cards.title: Terrorist financing: same discipline, separate law
cards.body:
The Terrorism Act 2000 makes it an offence to raise, receive, provide, use or possess money for terrorism (ss.15 and 16), to be involved in funding arrangements (s.17) and to help someone keep or control terrorist property (s.18). The test is often **reasonable cause to suspect**, and amounts can be small.

In the regulated sector, s.21A makes it an offence not to disclose knowledge or suspicion of these offences to a constable or the nominated officer as soon as practicable. Use the **same internal reporting route**, and say clearly that you suspect terrorist financing.

cards.title: Stage 3 take-aways
items: Report internally to the nominated officer as soon as practicable; the nominated officer decides on SARs to the NCA's UKFIU.
A DAML request seeks consent for a specific act: seven working days' notice period, then a 31-day moratorium if refused.
Courts can extend the moratorium in 31-day steps, up to 186 days in total beyond the first 31.
Tipping off (s.333A, TA s.21D) means revealing a disclosure or investigation in a way likely to prejudice it; up to two years.
Terrorist financing has its own offences and disclosure duty under the Terrorism Act 2000, with the same internal route.

cards.prompt: Write the two sentences you would say if a customer asked you why their payment was delayed while a disclosure was pending. Do they reveal anything about a report or investigation? Would your MLRO approve them?

quiz.question: Priya decides a SAR is needed on Brightmoor Motors but the bank also wants to process the GBP 180,000 payment. What should the SAR include so that it works as a DAML request?
options: A statement that the bank is certain the funds are criminal property, supported by evidence of the underlying crime and the customer's involvement
The customer's written agreement to the disclosure
A clear description of the specific act the bank wants to do, such as the payment details, with the reasons for suspicion
A request for the NCA to investigate within 31 days
quiz.explanation: Consent covers a prohibited act, so the request must say exactly what the bank wants to do. Certainty is not required, the customer must never be told, and the 31-day period is a moratorium that follows a refusal, not an investigation deadline.

quiz.question: The NCA has not replied to a DAML request after seven working days, counted from the first working day after disclosure. What is the bank's legal position?
options: The bank must wait a further 31 days before acting
The bank must chase the NCA and cannot act without written consent
The bank is treated as having appropriate consent to do the act described in the disclosure
The request lapses and the bank must close the account
quiz.explanation: Under s.335(2) and (3), if no refusal arrives before the end of the notice period, consent is treated as given. The 31-day moratorium only starts if consent is refused. Before acting, the bank should still consider whether anything else, such as new information or a sanctions issue, prevents it.

quiz.question: The NCA refuses consent on day five of the notice period. When does the moratorium start and how long is it?
options: It starts at the end of the seven working days and lasts 31 working days, after which the bank must ask the NCA again for consent
It starts on the day the refusal notice is received and lasts 31 days, unless a court extends it
It starts on the date of the original disclosure and lasts 60 days
It lasts until the NCA decides, with no fixed limit
quiz.explanation: Section 335(6) sets a 31-day moratorium starting with the day the refusal notice is received. Section 336A allows court extensions of up to 31 days each, capped at 186 days in total beyond the first 31.

quiz.question: A nominated officer receives an internal report giving clear grounds for suspicion but decides not to make a SAR because the customer is profitable. Which offence is the nominated officer most at risk of?
options: Failure to disclose by a nominated officer in the regulated sector under POCA s.331
Tipping off under s.333A
No offence, because nominated officers have discretion
Breach of regulation 40 record keeping, because the nominated officer failed to keep the internal report on the customer's file
quiz.explanation: Section 331 applies to the nominated officer who receives a s.330 report and has knowledge, suspicion or reasonable grounds, but does not disclose as soon as practicable. Commercial value is not a reasonable excuse.

quiz.question: A customer asks a cashier why his account was frozen. The cashier says: 'I can't say, but you might want to speak to a solicitor about the police.' A disclosure had been made. What is the main legal risk?
options: Tipping off, because the remark reveals a likely investigation in a way that may prejudice it
Breach of data protection only
No risk, because the cashier refused to give details
Failure to disclose under s.330
quiz.explanation: Hinting at police involvement can reveal that an investigation is contemplated or under way. Whether it is an offence depends on whether it is likely to prejudice an investigation, but the remark creates exactly that risk.

quiz.question: Which statement about the s.330 'required disclosure' is correct?
options: It must prove which crime generated the funds
It includes the suspect's identity if known, where the laundered property is (as far as known) and the information behind the suspicion
It must include a signed statement from the customer
It is satisfied by telling your line manager verbally, as long as the line manager then passes the concern on to the nominated officer within 30 days
quiz.explanation: Section 330(5) sets out the content of the required disclosure. No proof of a specific crime is needed, the customer is never involved, and the recipient must be the nominated officer or an authorised NCA officer.

quiz.question: A payments analyst has reasonable cause to suspect that a small donation to a charity is going to fund a terrorist group. Under which law, and to whom, must she disclose?
options: Terrorism Act 2000 s.21A: disclose to the nominated officer or a constable as soon as practicable
POCA s.330 only, by reporting to the FCA within 30 days, because terrorist financing is a form of money laundering in UK law
No duty, because the amount is small
The sanctions regulations, by reporting to OFSI only
quiz.explanation: Section 21A creates the regulated-sector disclosure duty for terrorist financing, owed to a constable or nominated officer. There is no minimum amount. If a designated person is involved, an OFSI report may also be needed, but that does not replace the s.21A duty.

quiz.question: In the Stunt & Co case (2025), what did the FCA criticise Barclays for after it received information from law enforcement?
options: Making too many SARs, which overwhelmed the NCA
Not properly considering the money laundering risk, even after learning police had raided the firms involved
Tipping off the customer about the police raid
Refusing to provide information to the police during their investigation of Fowler Oldfield, and delaying its response to a production order
quiz.explanation: The FCA said Barclays failed to properly consider the risks even after law enforcement information and the raids, and reviewed its exposure only after learning of the NatWest prosecution. Information from law enforcement should trigger an immediate review.

quiz.question: Under POCA, a deposit-taking body operating an account does not commit a principal offence for an act involving criminal property below a threshold amount. What is the default amount set in s.339A?
options: GBP 1,000 in every case
GBP 10,000 in every case
There is no threshold for banks
GBP 3,000, unless a higher amount is specified by an officer
quiz.explanation: Section 339A sets a default threshold of GBP 3,000 for acts by deposit-taking bodies in operating an account, which a constable or customs officer may raise. It does not remove the duty to report suspicion under s.330.

quiz.question: Callum is unsure whether a customer's explanation removes his suspicion. He asks his branch colleagues for a vote. What is the problem with this approach?
options: None, because a majority view protects him from liability
It is fine as long as the customer is not present
He should instead ask the customer to confirm the explanation in writing, and only report if the customer refuses or the explanation does not match the account
Suspicion is personal and must go to the nominated officer; sharing it widely risks confidentiality and tipping off
quiz.explanation: The s.330 duty attaches to the person who has the knowledge or suspicion. Sharing it widely risks leaks. Getting the customer to confirm in writing does not remove a suspicion that already exists.

sessions.title: Financial Sanctions, OFSI and Proliferation Financing
sessions.summary: Handle sanctions screening hits, asset freezes and OFSI reporting, apply the ownership and control test, and bring proliferation financing into everyday controls.
objectives: Explain how sanctions regulations under SAMLA 2018 and the UK Sanctions List work
Apply asset freeze prohibitions, including the ownership and control test
Report to OFSI and distinguish OFSI reports from SARs to the NCA
Recognise proliferation financing warning signs and the regulation 18A and 19A duties

cards.title: A name on the list
cards.setting: Payments screening desk, Larkhill Bank, Birmingham. Thursday, 7:55 am.

lines.text: Two screening hits before my coffee. A GBP 72,000 payment to 'Volkov Trading', and a name match on the beneficiary's director.
And Volkov Trading is 60% owned by a man on the UK Sanctions List. The company itself isn't listed.
If the company isn't on the list, can't we just pay? The client is a good exporter.

Not so fast. Ownership and control can bring an unlisted company inside an asset freeze. And trade finance has flagged a letter of credit for precision machine tools to a freight forwarder with no clear end user.
Sanctions and proliferation financing in one morning. Different laws, different reporting lines.
Stage 4. By lunchtime you'll know when to freeze, who to tell and how proliferation financing fits into our MLR duties.

scenes.heading: The legal base
scenes.narration: The Sanctions and Anti-Money Laundering Act 2018 lets ministers make sanctions regulations, regime by regime, for purposes such as national security, counter-terrorism and international peace.

scenes.heading: One list to screen against
scenes.narration: The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office publishes the UK Sanctions List, which names those designated or specified under the regulations.

scenes.heading: What an asset freeze means
scenes.narration: You must not deal with funds or economic resources of a designated person, must not make funds available to them or for their benefit, and must not help anyone get around the rules. Freeze immediately.

scenes.heading: Owned or controlled
scenes.narration: The freeze also reaches entities a designated person owns or controls, for example through more than 50% of the shares or voting rights, or the right to appoint most of the board.

scenes.heading: Tell OFSI
scenes.narration: Banks are relevant firms. They must tell OFSI as soon as practicable if they know or reasonably suspect someone is a designated person or that a breach has happened, using information gained in business.

cards.title: Handling a screening hit
cards.caption: Your bank's procedures set who can discount alerts and how decisions are recorded.

items.label: Alert raised
items.detail: Screening flags a payment, customer or counterparty.

items.label: Compare identifiers
items.detail: Dates of birth, addresses, registration numbers, nationality, ownership.

items.label: Decide the match
items.detail: False positive, possible match needing more data, or true match.

items.label: True match: stop and freeze
items.detail: Do not process; hold funds and economic resources.

items.label: Report to OFSI
items.detail: As soon as practicable, with what you know and what you hold.

items.label: Licence or release
items.detail: Act only under an OFSI licence or exception; record every decision.

cards.title: Freeze, discount or dig deeper?
cards.prompt: Sort each screening outcome into the right action.

items.text: Exact match on name, date of birth and passport number of a designated person
A company 70% owned by a designated individual
Same common surname, but a different date of birth and nationality
A name match where the listed person died before the account was opened, confirmed by the record
A partial name match with no date of birth on the payment message
A company whose 45% shareholder is designated and may control its board

cards.question: Volkov Trading is not itself on the UK Sanctions List, but a designated person owns 60% of its shares. What follows?
options: Nothing, because only listed names are frozen
It is treated as owned or controlled by the designated person, so the asset freeze reaches it
The bank may pay if the amount is under GBP 100,000
The bank must ask the customer whether the owner is involved
cards.explanation: OFSI guidance says an entity is owned or controlled by a designated person if, among other tests, that person holds more than 50% of the shares or voting rights. Funds must not be made available to it without a licence.

cards.title: Two reports, two channels
cards.body:
Sanctions and money laundering run on **separate legal tracks**:

- **OFSI** (HM Treasury) receives reports under the sanctions regulations: suspected designated persons, frozen assets and breaches. Failing to report is itself an offence.
- **The NCA's UKFIU** receives SARs under POCA and the Terrorism Act.

One event can need **both**. If a designated person tries to move money through a front company, the bank freezes and reports to OFSI, and the nominated officer considers a SAR.

**Licences.** OFSI can license activity that would otherwise be prohibited, for example basic needs or legal fees. Do not act until a licence is in place and its conditions are met.

**Penalties.** Breaching the main prohibitions is a crime, with up to **seven years' imprisonment** on indictment, and OFSI can impose monetary penalties. Anyone holding frozen funds on **30 September** must report them to OFSI for the **annual frozen assets review** by **30 November**.

cards.title: Sanctions vocabulary
cards.prompt: Match each term to its meaning in UK financial sanctions.

pairs.right: Someone named under UK sanctions regulations and listed on the UK Sanctions List
A ban on dealing with, or making available, funds and economic resources of a designated person
Written permission from OFSI for activity that would otherwise be prohibited
A business, such as a bank, with a legal duty to report knowledge or suspicion to OFSI
Tests, such as holding over 50% of shares, that extend a freeze to unlisted entities
Acting to get around the prohibitions, itself prohibited

cards.title: The machine tools letter of credit
cards.setting: Trade finance office, London. Thursday, 11:20 am.

lines.text: The letter of credit is for a long-standing exporter. Precision machine tools, GBP 640,000. It's good business.
The buyer is a freight forwarder in a transit country. The goods description is vague, and the end user is 'to be advised'.
Machine tools can be dual-use. Since 2022 our MLR risk assessment and training must cover proliferation financing as well as laundering and terrorist financing.
And the FATF call-for-action list is now the trigger for enhanced due diligence on country risk, after the 2026 amendments.
So what do we actually do, today?

cards.title: SAR to the NCA or report to OFSI?
cards.caption: When both apply, do both. Your MLRO and sanctions team coordinate.

items.label: Trigger
items.left: Knowledge, suspicion or reasonable grounds about ML or TF
items.right: Knowledge or reasonable suspicion of a designated person or breach

items.label: Internal route
items.right: Report under the bank's sanctions procedure

items.label: Can the bank proceed?
items.left: Only with consent or after the statutory periods
items.right: Only under an OFSI licence or exception

items.label: Tipping off rules
items.right: Follow OFSI guidance and bank policy on confidentiality

cards.title: Dual-use goods, unclear end user
cards.situation: The GBP 640,000 letter of credit covers precision machine tools sold to a freight forwarder in a transit country. No party screens as a designated person. The end user is 'to be advised', the goods description is vague, and the route is unusual for the product. Tom wants it issued today.

choices.text: Hold the transaction, ask for end-user information and any export licence, escalate under the bank's proliferation financing procedure, and involve the MLRO
choices.outcome: Best answer. Regulations 18A and 19A require PF risk to be assessed and controlled, and these are classic warning signs. Holding while you gather facts is proportionate; if suspicion remains, the MLRO considers disclosure.

choices.text: Issue it: no party is on the UK Sanctions List, so there is no legal issue
choices.outcome: Screening clear is not the same as risk clear. Proliferation financing often uses unlisted intermediaries. Ignoring the warning signs fails the PF controls the MLRs require.

choices.text: Reject it outright and tell the exporter the bank suspects weapons proliferation
choices.outcome: Rejecting may be right in the end, but telling the customer what the bank suspects risks tipping off if a disclosure follows. Gather facts first and keep concerns internal.

choices.text: Issue it but add the customer to a watch list for future trades
choices.outcome: Monitoring helps, but issuing now leaves the current risk unmanaged. Partly right at best.

cards.title: Real case: Starling Bank (2024)
cards.body:
In October 2024 the FCA fined **Starling Bank Limited** about **GBP 29.0m** (GBP 28,959,426) for financial crime failings linked to its financial sanctions screening.

- In January 2023 Starling found that its automated screening had, **since 2017, checked customers against only a fraction** of the full list of those subject to financial sanctions.
- An internal review found systemic issues in its sanctions framework, and Starling reported multiple potential breaches to the authorities.
- Under a requirement not to open accounts for high-risk customers, it opened **more than 54,000** accounts for about **49,000** high-risk customers between 2021 and 2023.
- The fine reflects a 30% settlement discount from about GBP 41.0m.

**Lesson:** test that screening covers the whole list, every day. Source: FCA press release, 2 October 2024.

cards.back: Providing funds or financial services that help develop, acquire or deliver weapons of mass destruction or their means of delivery, often through dual-use goods and front companies.
The bank must identify and assess its proliferation financing risks.
The bank must have policies, controls and procedures to manage those PF risks.
Training must cover PF law and how to recognise and deal with PF-related activity.
Many PF-related designations are made under UK sanctions regulations, so screening and OFSI reporting are part of PF controls.
FATF sets the global standard, and since 30 June 2026 its call-for-action list drives EDD on country risk under regulation 33.

cards.question: Which lesson from the Starling case (2024) applies most directly to a sanctions screening team?
options: Screening only new customers is enough once the back book has been checked
Screening must cover the full current list, and its coverage should be tested
Screening can be paused when a bank is growing quickly
Only payments above GBP 10,000 need to be screened
cards.explanation: Starling's system had screened customers against only a fraction of the full sanctions list since 2017. Coverage and data completeness must be tested regularly. There is no minimum amount for sanctions.

cards.title: Sanctions numbers to remember
cards.caption: From OFSI's general guidance (updated May 2026) and the FCA's Starling press release.

items.label: Ownership test
items.detail: Holding over this share of shares or voting rights means 'owned'.

items.label: Maximum prison term
items.detail: For breaching the main prohibitions, on indictment.

items.label: Frozen assets review
items.detail: Annual deadline for reporting funds held frozen on 30 September.

items.label: Starling fine (2024)
items.detail: FCA fine linked to sanctions screening failures.

cards.title: Stage 4 take-aways
items: UK sanctions regulations are made under SAMLA 2018; the FCDO publishes the UK Sanctions List and OFSI enforces financial sanctions.
An asset freeze covers designated persons and entities they own or control, including over 50% ownership; freeze immediately.
Banks are relevant firms: report knowledge or reasonable suspicion to OFSI as soon as practicable, and act only under a licence.
OFSI reports and SARs to the NCA are separate; one case may need both.
Regulations 18A, 19A and 24 bring proliferation financing into the bank's risk assessment, controls and training.

cards.prompt: Think about the payments or trade transactions you handle. Where could an unlisted company owned by a designated person, or a dual-use shipment, slip through? What extra question would you ask?

quiz.question: A payment to Volkov Trading is held. Volkov is not listed, but a designated person owns 60% of it. The customer says it is a routine supplier payment. What should Sana do?
options: Process it, because Volkov is not named on the UK Sanctions List
Process it if the customer signs an indemnity
Treat it as caught by the asset freeze: do not process it, and report to OFSI as soon as practicable
Return the funds to the customer, record the alert as a possible match and close the case without reporting, since Volkov is not itself designated
quiz.explanation: Under OFSI's ownership and control test, more than 50% ownership by a designated person brings the entity within the freeze. The bank must not make funds available and, as a relevant firm, must report. An indemnity does not change the law.

quiz.question: Who publishes the UK Sanctions List that banks screen against?
options: The FCA, as part of its supervision of financial crime controls
The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO)
The NCA's UK Financial Intelligence Unit
The Bank of England's PRA
quiz.explanation: OFSI's guidance says the FCDO publishes the UK Sanctions List. OFSI enforces financial sanctions; the FCA supervises firms' controls.

quiz.question: A screening analyst confirms a true match on a customer who holds a savings account. What are the immediate obligations?
options: Freeze the funds, do not deal with them or make funds available, and report to OFSI as soon as practicable
Close the account at once and send the balance back to the customer's nominated account, then report the closure to OFSI
Ask the customer to confirm whether they are designated
Wait until the next annual frozen assets review to report
quiz.explanation: Funds must be frozen immediately and OFSI told as soon as practicable. Paying the balance out would make funds available to a designated person. The annual review is an extra duty, not a substitute for prompt reporting.

quiz.question: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between OFSI reports and SARs?
options: An OFSI report automatically counts as a SAR
They are separate duties under different laws; one event can require both an OFSI report and a SAR to the NCA
A SAR to the NCA automatically satisfies the OFSI reporting duty, because the NCA shares every SAR with OFSI and HM Treasury
Banks report sanctions breaches only to the FCA
quiz.explanation: OFSI reporting comes from the sanctions regulations; SARs come from POCA and the Terrorism Act. Neither replaces the other, so banks coordinate both.

quiz.question: A trade finance officer sees a letter of credit for dual-use goods with an unclear end user, routed through a transit hub. No party is designated. Which MLR provisions make this a matter for the bank's controls?
options: Regulation 40, which covers record keeping only
Regulations 18A and 19A, which require a proliferation financing risk assessment and matching policies and controls
None, because proliferation financing is only a sanctions issue
Regulation 27, which sets the GBP 12,000 occasional transaction threshold
quiz.explanation: Regulations 18A and 19A bring PF risk into the bank's risk assessment and controls, and regulation 24 training covers it. PF is wider than screening against names.

quiz.question: A designated person's lawyer asks the bank to pay legal fees from frozen funds. What is the correct approach?
options: Pay, because legal fees are always exempt from asset freezes
Pay, if the lawyer is regulated in the UK
Do not pay unless an OFSI licence (or a relevant exception) covers the payment, and follow its conditions
Refuse permanently, because frozen funds can never be released
quiz.explanation: OFSI can license otherwise prohibited activity, such as legal fees, but the bank must have the licence (or rely on a valid exception) before acting. Frozen funds are not confiscated and can be released lawfully.

quiz.question: What is the maximum prison sentence on indictment for breaching the main prohibitions of UK financial sanctions, according to OFSI's guidance?
options: Two years
Fourteen years
Five years
Seven years
quiz.explanation: OFSI's guidance states a maximum of seven years on indictment for offences relating to the principal prohibitions. Two years is the maximum for tipping off; fourteen years applies to the POCA principal laundering offences.

quiz.question: In the Starling case (2024), what did the bank discover about its sanctions screening in January 2023?
options: Since 2017 its automated system had screened customers against only a fraction of the full sanctions list
It had screened against the full list throughout, but had never reported any of the matches it found to OFSI or the FCA
Its screening had been switched off for international payments only
It had screened only staff, not customers
quiz.explanation: The FCA said Starling's automated system had checked customers against only part of the full sanctions list since 2017, revealing systemic issues in its framework.

quiz.question: A company has three shareholders: a designated person with 40%, and two unconnected investors with 30% each. The designated person also has the right to appoint most of the board. Is the company 'owned or controlled' by the designated person?
options: No, because the designated person holds less than 50% of the shares, and OFSI's ownership and control test looks only at shareholdings and voting rights
Only if the designated person is also a director
Only if the company is registered in the UK
Yes: the right to appoint or remove most of the board meets the control test without a majority shareholding
quiz.explanation: OFSI's guidance treats the right to appoint or remove a majority of the board as one way of meeting the ownership and control test. Shareholding below 50% does not settle the question.

quiz.question: A bank holds frozen funds of a designated person on 30 September. By what date must it report them to OFSI for the annual frozen assets review?
options: 30 November
31 October
31 December
31 December, the end of the calendar year
quiz.explanation: OFSI's guidance says the annual reporting deadline moved from 31 October to 30 November from 2025 onwards. Failing to comply without reasonable excuse is an offence.

sessions.title: The Firm's Programme: MLRO, Training, Accountability and Records
sessions.summary: Prepare for the final exam and an FCA visit: governance roles, regulation 24 training, record keeping, senior manager accountability, the 2026 amendments and enforcement.
objectives: Describe the regulation 21 roles: responsible officer, nominated officer, screening and audit
Design and evidence regulation 24 training for relevant employees and agents
Apply regulation 40 retention and deletion rules
Explain FCA enforcement under regulations 76 and 86 and senior manager accountability

cards.title: The FCA is coming
cards.setting: Boardroom, Larkhill Bank, Manchester. Friday, 8:30 am.

lines.text: The FCA has asked for our financial crime risk assessment, training records and the MLRO annual report. Their visit is in three weeks.
I'm the senior manager with financial crime in my responsibilities. What does that actually mean for me, personally?
And Callum says half his new cashiers started serving customers before their AML module. Do we have a record problem?
We trained them in their second week. Is that not good enough?
Final stage. Today we prove Larkhill has a programme, not just policies: clear owners, real training, solid records and controls that work.

cards.title: The firm's AML programme under the MLRs

scenes.heading: A named owner at the top
scenes.narration: Where appropriate to its size and nature, the bank must appoint a board member or senior manager as the officer responsible for its compliance with the Regulations.

scenes.heading: A nominated officer
scenes.narration: The bank must appoint a nominated officer to receive internal reports and decide on disclosures. The FCA must be told who holds both roles within 14 days of appointment.

scenes.heading: Screening and audit
scenes.narration: Relevant employees must be screened before appointment and during it, for skills, knowledge, conduct and integrity. Where appropriate, an independent audit function tests the controls.

scenes.heading: Training under regulation 24
scenes.narration: Relevant employees, and agents doing similar work, must be made aware of the law on laundering, terrorist financing, proliferation financing and data protection, and trained regularly to recognise and deal with suspicious activity.

scenes.heading: Records that prove it
scenes.narration: The bank must keep a written record of the training and other measures it takes, as well as CDD and transaction records for the periods the Regulations set.

cards.title: Who is accountable at Larkhill
cards.caption: Under the SM&CR, named senior managers also carry personal responsibility for financial crime controls.

items.label: Board and senior management
items.detail: Approve policies, controls and procedures (reg 19) and set the risk appetite.

items.label: Officer responsible for MLR compliance
items.detail: Board member or senior manager accountable for compliance (reg 21(1)(a)).

items.label: MLRO and nominated officer
items.detail: Receives internal reports, decides on SARs and DAML requests, reports to the board.

items.label: Business lines
items.detail: Apply CDD, monitor customers and report suspicion.

items.label: Independent audit
items.detail: Tests whether controls are adequate and effective, and tracks fixes.

cards.title: Match the regulation to the duty
cards.prompt: Link each MLR 2017 provision to the duty it sets.

pairs.right: Firm-wide written ML and TF risk assessment
Responsible officer, nominated officer, staff screening and independent audit
Awareness and regular training for relevant employees and agents, with a written record
Stop and end the relationship when CDD cannot be completed
Keep CDD and transaction records for at least five years
FCA power to impose penalties or publish a statement of censure

cards.question: A business relationship ended on 1 March 2026. Under regulation 40, for how long must the bank normally keep the CDD records?
options: At least five years from when the bank knows or has reasonable grounds to believe the relationship ended
Seven years from account opening
Indefinitely, in case of future investigations
Until the next FCA visit
cards.explanation: Regulation 40(3) sets at least five years from the end of the relationship (or completion of an occasional transaction). Transaction records within a relationship need not be kept more than ten years, and after the period personal data must be deleted unless an exception applies.

cards.title: FCA expectations: SYSC and the SM&CR in brief
cards.body:
The FCA supervises banks for compliance with the MLRs and with its own Handbook. In general terms:

- **SYSC 6.3** expects banks to have systems and controls that identify, assess, monitor and manage money laundering risk in proportion to the business, and an MLRO with sufficient authority to do the job.
- **The Senior Managers and Certification Regime** gives named senior managers responsibility for areas such as financial crime. They are expected to take reasonable steps to prevent breaches in their area.
- **Competence** rules expect staff to have the skills and knowledge their role requires.

Check the current Handbook and your bank's responsibilities map for the exact rules: the FCA has been consulting on changes to parts of the SM&CR in 2026.

Under the MLRs themselves, the FCA can fine a bank or publish a censure (reg 76), and can also fine an officer **knowingly concerned** in the bank's breach.

cards.title: Building a regulation 24 training cycle
cards.prompt: Put the steps of a sound annual AML training cycle in order.
steps: Identify relevant employees and agents whose work affects AML compliance or detection
Map the risks each role faces, using the firm-wide risk assessment
Design content covering ML, TF and PF law, data protection and how to spot and report suspicion
Deliver training before customer contact for new joiners, then regularly for everyone
Test understanding and follow up on gaps
Record in writing who was trained, on what and when
Review effectiveness against SARs, audit findings and new risks, then update

lines.text: Budgets are tight. What if we train people once at induction and drop the refresher? And cut two monitoring analysts while we're at it.
Regulation 24 says relevant employees must be trained regularly, not once. And our risk assessment drives the monitoring headcount.
Remember HSBC's fine: monitoring scenarios and parameters not tested for years. Starving controls is how that happens.
And if the FCA finds a breach in my area, I'm the one answering for it.
Exactly. Let's make a decision we can defend.

cards.title: The budget decision
cards.situation: Tom must cut costs by 10%. His proposal: (1) AML training only at induction; (2) remove two transaction monitoring analysts; (3) keep the alert thresholds unchanged. Alert backlogs are already rising. Priya, as MLRO, is asked for her view before the executive committee meets.

choices.text: Advise against both cuts, explain the regulation 24 and risk assessment links, propose efficiencies such as better alert tuning tested against risk, and record the advice for the board
choices.outcome: Best answer. The MLRO's job is to give clear, documented advice. Regular training is a legal duty, and monitoring resources must match assessed risk. Smarter tuning, tested properly, can save money without weakening controls.

choices.text: Agree to both cuts to keep good relations with the business
choices.outcome: Training only at induction breaches the 'regularly' requirement, and cutting analysts with rising backlogs weakens controls that must match the bank's risk. The MLRO would be failing in their role.

choices.text: Accept the training cut but resist the analyst cut
choices.outcome: Protecting monitoring is right, but induction-only training still fails regulation 24's duty to train regularly. Partly right.

choices.text: Say nothing now and raise concerns only if the FCA finds a problem
choices.outcome: Silence leaves the board uninformed and the MLRO exposed. Raising concerns early and in writing is part of the role.

cards.title: The 2026 amendments (SI 2026/621)
cards.caption: Regulation 24 (training) was not changed by SI 2026/621.

items.label: Made
items.detail: The Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing (Amendment) Regulations 2026 were made.

items.label: Most changes in force
items.detail: FATF call-for-action countries replace 'high-risk third country'; sterling CDD thresholds.

items.label: Regulation 34A
items.detail: Correspondent EDD for cryptoasset firms only; banks stay under reg 34.

items.label: Crypto change of control
items.detail: Further cryptoasset change-of-control rules.

cards.title: Real case: HSBC's transaction monitoring (2021)

cards.front: Regulation 76: what can the FCA do?
cards.back: Impose a penalty of the amount it considers appropriate, publish a statement censuring the firm, or both.
Yes. An officer knowingly concerned in the firm's contravention can be penalised personally.
No penalty if the firm took all reasonable steps and exercised all due diligence to comply.
Contravening a relevant requirement is a criminal offence, with up to two years' imprisonment on indictment.
Yes. Regulators and courts must consider whether the firm followed relevant guidance issued by the FCA or approved by the Treasury.

cards.front: First criminal MLR prosecution by the FCA
cards.back: NatWest, which pleaded guilty and was fined about GBP 264.8m in December 2021.

cards.question: Under regulation 76(4), when must the FCA not impose a penalty for a breach of the MLRs?
options: When the firm has already reported the breach to the NCA
When the breach was caused by a junior employee
When the firm took all reasonable steps and exercised all due diligence to ensure compliance
When the firm is a PRA-authorised bank
cards.explanation: Regulation 76(4) bars a penalty where the firm took all reasonable steps and exercised all due diligence. For PRA-authorised firms the FCA must consult the PRA, but it can still impose a penalty.
