cards.title: Stage 5 take-aways
items: Regulation 21: a responsible board member or senior manager, a nominated officer, staff screening and independent audit; tell the FCA within 14 days of appointments.
Regulation 24: make relevant employees and agents aware of ML, TF, PF and data protection law, train them regularly and keep a written record.
Regulation 40: keep CDD and transaction records for at least five years after the relationship ends, then delete personal data unless an exception applies.
The FCA can fine or censure firms and knowingly concerned officers (reg 76); breaches can also be prosecuted (reg 86).
SM&CR senior managers answer personally for financial crime controls in their area: resource them and test that they work.

cards.prompt: Imagine the FCA asks you tomorrow to show how your role's AML training links to your bank's risk assessment. What evidence could you show, and what is missing?

quiz.question: Larkhill appoints a new nominated officer on 2 March. Under regulation 21, what must the bank do about the FCA?
options: Ask the FCA to approve the appointment before it takes effect
Notify the FCA at the next annual return
Nothing, because only the MLR compliance officer must be notified
Inform the FCA of the appointment within 14 days
quiz.explanation: Regulation 21(4) requires the bank to tell its supervisor the identity of the responsible officer and the nominated officer, and of any later appointments, within 14 days. Separate SM&CR approval rules may also apply to senior roles.

quiz.question: Callum's new cashiers served customers for a week before completing AML training. Which regulation 24 element is most directly at risk?
options: The duty to appoint a nominated officer
The duty to keep transaction records for five years
Making relevant employees aware of the law and training them to recognise and deal with suspicious activity
The duty to report frozen funds and economic resources to OFSI in the annual frozen assets review
quiz.explanation: Cashiers are relevant employees. Regulation 24 requires awareness and regular training, and good practice is to train people for their role before they serve customers. The other duties are real but are not the issue here.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a 'relevant employee' for regulation 24 purposes?
options: Only staff in the compliance department
Only staff who handle cash or make payments for customers, since they are the people who can see suspicious transactions
Only staff at manager grade and above
Anyone whose work affects MLR compliance or can help identify, mitigate, prevent or detect ML, TF or PF
quiz.explanation: Regulation 24(2) defines relevant employees by the nature of their work, which covers front-line, operations and many support roles, not just compliance or cash staff.

quiz.question: Tom proposes training staff only at induction to save money. Why does this conflict with the MLRs?
options: Regulation 24 requires relevant employees to be given training regularly, not just once
Regulation 24 requires training every month
Regulation 24 requires training to be delivered by the FCA
Regulation 24 only applies to agents, not employees
quiz.explanation: The regulation requires regular training. It does not set a fixed frequency, so the bank decides, using its size, nature and risks, how often 'regularly' means. One-off training does not meet it.

quiz.question: A customer relationship ended in 2019. The bank still holds the customer's CDD file in 2026 and no exception applies. What does regulation 40 require?
options: Delete the personal data, because the five-year retention period has expired and no exception applies
Keep it indefinitely for possible future investigations
Keep it for ten years from account opening, because the MLRs set a single fixed retention period for all customer records
Send it to the NCA for archiving
quiz.explanation: After the retention period, regulation 40(5) requires personal data obtained for MLR purposes to be deleted unless a statutory exception applies, such as another legal requirement, court proceedings or consent. Data protection and AML duties work together.

quiz.question: An FCA investigation finds that a senior executive knowingly allowed a breach of the MLRs in her bank. What can the FCA do under regulation 76?
options: Nothing, because only the firm can be penalised under the MLRs; individuals can only be dealt with under the SM&CR
Only issue a private warning
Impose a penalty on her personally as an officer knowingly concerned in the contravention
Only refer her to the NCA
quiz.explanation: Regulation 76(3) allows the FCA to penalise an officer knowingly concerned in the firm's contravention. This sits alongside the SM&CR, which also holds senior managers accountable for their areas.

quiz.question: In the HSBC case (2021), which of the following was NOT one of the transaction monitoring weaknesses the FCA described?
options: Failing to appoint a nominated officer to review alerts
Not checking whether monitoring scenarios covered the relevant risks
Not properly testing and updating the parameters that flagged suspicious transactions
Not checking the accuracy and completeness of data feeding the systems
quiz.explanation: The FCA described weaknesses in scenario coverage, parameter testing and data quality. It did not say HSBC lacked a nominated officer.

quiz.question: Which statement about SI 2026/621 is correct?
options: It replaced the Money Laundering Regulations 2017 with a completely new set of regulations from 30 June 2026
Most changes took effect on 30 June 2026, and it did not amend the regulation 24 training duty
It abolished the nominated officer role
It introduced a fixed annual training requirement
quiz.explanation: The 2026 amendments are targeted changes, mostly in force from 30 June 2026, with later dates for some cryptoasset provisions. They left regulation 24 unchanged.

quiz.question: Under regulation 21, which statement about the independent audit function is correct?
options: It must be outsourced to an external auditor every year
Where appropriate, the bank must have one that examines AML controls, recommends fixes and monitors follow-up
It replaces the need for a nominated officer, because auditors review all internal suspicion reports and decide which ones to send to the NCA
It is only needed if the FCA requests it
quiz.explanation: Regulation 21(1)(c) describes an independent audit function that examines adequacy and effectiveness of controls, recommends improvements and monitors compliance with them. It is proportionate to size and nature and does not have to be external.

quiz.question: Priya's annual MLRO report says monitoring backlogs are rising. The executive committee ignores it. What is the best next step for Priya?
options: Stop reviewing alerts until more staff are hired
Escalate in writing to the board and the responsible senior manager, setting out the risk and options
Report the bank to the NCA for failing to resource AML
Quietly raise the alert thresholds so the backlog shrinks, and explain the change in next year's MLRO report once staffing has recovered
quiz.explanation: The MLRO must make sure those accountable understand the risk. Escalating with a record is right. Stopping reviews or raising thresholds without risk testing would weaken controls, and the NCA is not the channel for governance concerns.

bank.question: A Larkhill mortgage adviser suspects that a deposit for a house purchase comes from a relative's fraud. She completes the mortgage anyway and makes no report. Which statement best describes her exposure?
options: She risks only a regulatory breach of the bank's lending policy, because the fraud was committed by a relative and not by the mortgage customer
She risks a principal offence under s.328 for being concerned in an arrangement, and the s.330 failure-to-disclose offence
She risks only tipping off, because she said nothing to the customer
She has no exposure unless the relative is later convicted of fraud
bank.explanation: Completing a mortgage she suspects helps another person use criminal property is a s.328 arrangement, and failing to report risks s.330. No conviction is needed for property to be criminal; tipping off requires a disclosure, which did not happen here.

bank.question: Under POCA, which element distinguishes the s.330 failure-to-disclose offence from the principal offences in ss.327 to 329?
options: It applies only to cash transactions above a threshold
It requires proof that the employee personally benefited
It can only be committed by the nominated officer, because front-line staff discharge their duty by telling their line manager
It can be committed on reasonable grounds to know or suspect, not only actual knowledge or suspicion
bank.explanation: Section 330 includes an objective limb (reasonable grounds), whereas the principal offences turn on the person knowing or suspecting the property is criminal. It applies to anyone in the regulated sector, not just nominated officers, and needs no personal benefit or threshold.

bank.question: A cashier made an internal report about a customer before processing a cash deposit, and the nominated officer then sought and received appropriate consent. Which statement is correct?
options: The cashier is still guilty of s.329 because she handled the cash
The defence only works if the disclosure was made directly to the NCA, so a report to the nominated officer gives no protection at all
The authorised disclosure plus appropriate consent gives a defence to the principal offences for that act
Consent from the nominated officer is never valid
bank.explanation: Under ss.327-329 and s.338, an authorised disclosure to a nominated officer, with appropriate consent before the act, is a defence. Section 335(1)(a) recognises the nominated officer's consent where the disclosure is made to them, though the nominated officer will usually need NCA consent first.

bank.question: A customer's money came from conduct abroad that was lawful in that country and is not of a description prescribed by the Secretary of State, although it would be an offence in the UK. A Larkhill employee knows this. Which is correct?
options: POCA never applies to any conduct outside the UK
The money is automatically criminal property and no defence can ever apply, because UK law treats all overseas conduct as if it happened in the UK
Only OFSI can decide whether such funds may be handled
POCA has a defence where the conduct is known or reasonably believed to have been lawful where it occurred and is not of a prescribed kind
bank.explanation: Criminal conduct includes overseas conduct that would be an offence in the UK, but ss.327(2A), 328(3) and 329(2A) contain an overseas-conduct defence where the conduct was lawful where it occurred and is not prescribed. The defence is narrow and should be judged with the MLRO.

bank.question: Which statement about the legal status of the Money Laundering Regulations 2017 is correct?
options: They are voluntary guidance with no penalties attached
They apply only to cryptoasset firms since the 2026 amendments moved banks back under the Financial Services and Markets Act
Breaches can lead to an FCA civil penalty (reg 76) or a criminal prosecution (reg 86)
Breaches can only be punished by OFSI
bank.explanation: The MLRs carry civil penalties (reg 76) and a criminal offence (reg 86, up to two years on indictment). NatWest's 2021 conviction under the 2007 Regulations shows the criminal route is used. OFSI enforces sanctions, not the MLRs.

bank.question: In the NatWest case, branch staff had reported red flags about Fowler Oldfield's cash deposits. What does the outcome teach about a bank's internal reporting system?
options: Banks are protected from prosecution once any staff member reports
The bank's failing was that staff reported too many concerns
Internal reports are irrelevant if a monitoring system exists
Reports must be properly investigated and acted on; staff reporting alone did not protect the bank
bank.explanation: The FCA said staff reported suspicions but no appropriate action followed, and monitoring misclassified cash as cheques. Reporting is the start of the process, not the end.

bank.question: Santander's AML team recommended closing a suspicious business account in March 2014, but the closure only happened in September 2015. Which control weakness does this best illustrate?
options: The bank lacked a written risk assessment under regulation 18
The bank failed to screen the customer against the sanctions list
The bank tipped off the customer about its closure decision
Decisions on high-risk accounts were not tracked and executed, so known risks stayed open
bank.explanation: The FCA described poor processes and structures that meant the closure recommendation was not acted on for about 18 months. It is an execution and governance failure rather than a sanctions or tipping-off issue.

bank.question: A teller is told by a customer: 'I'm paying in my brother's drug money, but don't worry, it's only GBP 500.' The account belongs to the customer. Which is the most accurate statement?
options: The teller has knowledge and must report internally; the bank needs consent before dealing, subject to the account threshold rules
Nothing needs to happen because the amount is below every threshold
The teller should refuse the cash, explain to the customer that the bank will have to call the police, and then make an internal report
The teller should accept it and report only if a second deposit follows
bank.explanation: Knowledge triggers the s.330 duty to report as soon as practicable. Section 339A has a threshold for deposit-taking bodies operating accounts, but that affects the principal offences, not the duty to report. Threatening police contact risks tipping off.

bank.question: Which body supervises UK banks for compliance with the Money Laundering Regulations?
options: The Financial Conduct Authority
The National Crime Agency
OFSI at HM Treasury
Companies House
bank.explanation: The FCA is the supervisory authority for banks under the MLRs. The NCA receives SARs, OFSI enforces financial sanctions and Companies House runs the company register.

bank.question: Larkhill's risk assessment has not been updated since it launched a new instant cross-border payments app. Which requirements are most directly at risk?
options: Regulation 40 only, because records are incomplete
Regulation 35 only, because some app users may be PEPs
Regulation 18 (keep the risk assessment up to date) and regulation 19 (assess new products and technology)
None, because firm-wide risk assessments only need to be updated when the FCA asks for them during a supervisory visit or review
bank.explanation: Regulation 18 requires an up-to-date written record of the risk assessment, and regulation 19(4)(c) requires measures to assess and mitigate risks of new products, practices and technology. Waiting for the FCA would not meet either.

bank.question: A customer makes an occasional transaction (not a funds transfer) of GBP 11,500, and a linked one of GBP 900 a day later. There is no business relationship and no suspicion. Since 30 June 2026, must CDD be applied?
options: No, because each payment is below GBP 12,000
Yes, because linked operations totalling GBP 12,000 or more trigger CDD for an occasional transaction
No, because the threshold is still EUR 15,000
Only if the second payment is in cash
bank.explanation: Regulation 27(2) counts operations that appear to be linked. Together they reach GBP 12,000, the sterling threshold introduced by SI 2026/621. Splitting a transaction does not avoid CDD.

bank.question: An overseas company's ownership is spread among many small shareholders, and despite exhausting all means the bank cannot identify a beneficial owner. What do the MLRs allow?
options: The bank may record 'no beneficial owner' and proceed with standard CDD
The bank must refuse the customer in every case
The bank may rely on the customer's signed declaration that there is no beneficial owner, provided the declaration is kept on file for five years
Treat the senior managing official as beneficial owner, verify that person and keep written records of the steps taken
bank.explanation: Regulation 28(6) to (8) permits the senior managing official fallback only after all possible means are exhausted, with reasonable verification and written records of the steps taken. Simply recording 'none' or accepting a declaration is not enough.

bank.question: Larkhill relies on a third-party firm established in a FATF call-for-action country to perform CDD. Under regulation 39 as amended, is this permitted?
options: Yes, as long as the third party is regulated in its home country
Yes, if the customer agrees in writing
No; a bank may not rely on a third party established in a FATF call-for-action country, subject to a narrow group exception
Yes, but only for customers rated low risk
bank.explanation: Regulation 39(4) bars reliance on a third party established in a FATF call-for-action country, with an exception for certain branches and majority-owned subsidiaries of group entities that meet conditions. Customer consent or local regulation does not change this.

bank.question: A non-domestic PEP's long-standing friend, who is known to jointly own a company with the PEP, opens an account. How should she be treated?
options: As a known close associate of a PEP, which brings regulation 35 EDD and senior management approval
As a standard customer, because only relatives are covered
As a PEP herself, with exactly the same treatment as the PEP in every respect, including after the PEP leaves office
As a prohibited person under sanctions law
bank.explanation: Regulation 35 defines known close associates to include someone known to have joint beneficial ownership of a legal entity with a PEP. They attract PEP measures, scaled to the risk.

bank.question: A domestic PEP customer is also linked to adverse media about procurement corruption. How does regulation 35(3A) apply?
options: The lower starting point applies, but adverse media is an enhanced risk factor that can justify more EDD
The lower starting point means EDD must stay light whatever the facts, because the law now treats all UK PEPs as presenting a lower risk
Domestic PEPs with adverse media must be exited immediately
Adverse media is irrelevant to PEP risk assessment
bank.explanation: Regulation 35(3A) sets a lower starting point and less EDD only where no enhanced risk factors are present. Factors other than PEP status, such as corruption allegations, can raise the risk and the EDD.

bank.question: Which statement about simplified due diligence (SDD) under regulation 37 is correct?
options: It may be applied only where the bank determines low risk, taking account of its risk assessment and the risk factors
SDD applies automatically to all UK resident individual customers, because the national risk assessment rates them as low risk
SDD means no identification is needed at all
SDD was abolished by SI 2026/621
bank.explanation: Regulation 37 permits SDD where the firm determines low risk, considering its regulation 18 risk assessment, supervisor information and risk factors. It is a judgment, not an automatic category, and it still involves CDD.

bank.question: A payment correspondent relationship is proposed with a respondent bank outside the UK. Which statement about regulation 34 and the 2026 amendments is correct for Larkhill?
options: Regulation 34 was repealed by SI 2026/621 and replaced by regulation 34A, which applies to banks and cryptoasset firms alike from 2027
No EDD applies if the respondent is in a FATF member country
Only OFSI can approve correspondent relationships
Regulation 34 enhanced measures apply; regulation 34A, from February 2027, is for cryptoasset firms, not banks
bank.explanation: Banks remain under regulation 34 for correspondent relationships with third-country respondents. SI 2026/621 adds regulation 34A from 1 February 2027 for cryptoasset exchange and custodian wallet providers.

bank.question: Monzo onboarded customers using obviously implausible details, such as famous London landmarks as home addresses. Which CDD element did this most clearly fail?
options: Verifying customer identity on the basis of reliable information and assessing whether the information was credible
Reporting frozen assets to OFSI
Keeping records for five years
Appointing a nominated officer
bank.explanation: Accepting implausible addresses shows weak identification and verification and weak customer risk assessment. The other options are real duties but not what the FCA highlighted.

bank.question: Priya sends a DAML request on Monday 22 December. Christmas Day and Boxing Day (a bank holiday) fall that week, and no other holidays apply. On which day does the seven-working-day notice period start?
options: Tuesday 23 December, the first working day after the disclosure
Monday 22 December, the day of the disclosure
Friday 2 January, after the holiday period
Monday 29 December, the start of the next full week
bank.explanation: Section 335(5) starts the notice period with the first working day after the disclosure. Christmas Day and bank holidays are excluded from the count, so they extend the end date, but the start is the next working day: Tuesday 23 December.

bank.question: The NCA refuses consent and a court later grants extensions of the moratorium. What is the overall limit on court extensions under s.336A?
options: There is no limit on extensions
Only one extension of 31 days is allowed
Extensions cannot total more than 186 days beyond the end of the original 31-day moratorium
Extensions are limited to 90 days in total
bank.explanation: Each extension may last up to 31 days, and s.336A(7) caps the total at 186 days beyond the first 31-day period. Applications must be made by a senior officer before the period ends.

bank.question: A Larkhill relationship manager tells a customer: 'Our compliance team has a few standard questions about the source of this payment.' A SAR was filed last week. Is this tipping off?
options: Yes, any contact with a customer after a SAR is tipping off
Yes, because mentioning compliance always reveals a SAR
No, because tipping off can only be committed by the nominated officer or by the employee who made the original internal report
Not in itself: routine CDD questions do not reveal a disclosure or investigation, but wording should be agreed with the MLRO
bank.explanation: Section 333A requires disclosure of a SAR or an investigation that is likely to prejudice it. Routine CDD questions do not reveal either, though wording should be careful and coordinated. Anyone in the regulated sector can commit the offence.

bank.question: A colleague asks Callum to explain why he made an internal report. Callum's manager has no role in the case. What should Callum do?
options: Share the details, because internal colleagues cannot commit tipping off
Share the details as long as the customer is not named
Delete his record of the report to protect confidentiality
Keep the details confidential and share them only with those in the nominated officer's need-to-know chain
bank.explanation: Internal gossip creates a risk that information reaches the customer, which could be tipping off by whoever passes it on. Records of internal reports should be kept, not deleted.

bank.question: The nominated officer receives an internal report but, after reviewing all the information, concludes there is no knowledge, suspicion or reasonable grounds. What should she do?
options: Make a SAR anyway, because every internal report must go to the NCA
Tell the reporting employee to withdraw the report
Record her reasoning for not making a SAR and keep the internal report on file
Inform the customer that the matter is closed
bank.explanation: Regulation 21(5) requires the nominated officer to consider reports in light of all relevant information and decide. If no suspicion results, she does not have to disclose, but should document why. Telling the customer would reveal the report.

bank.question: A payments analyst has reasonable grounds to suspect a customer is sending funds for a terrorist group but is unsure whether this is a POCA or Terrorism Act matter. What is the best approach?
options: Wait until it is clear which Act applies
Report internally to the nominated officer as soon as practicable, flagging the terrorist financing concern
Report only to OFSI, because terrorist financing is handled as a sanctions issue in the UK and not under the Terrorism Act's disclosure rules
Report only if the amount exceeds GBP 3,000
bank.explanation: Terrorism Act s.21A requires disclosure to a constable or nominated officer as soon as practicable, and banks use one internal route for both regimes. No threshold applies, and OFSI is not the TF reporting channel unless a designated person is involved.

bank.question: Brightmoor Motors' payment is pending a DAML decision. Tom, a senior manager, emails the branch: 'Release it, this customer is too valuable to lose.' What should happen?
options: The branch should follow Tom's instruction because he is senior
The payment stays held until consent or the statutory periods allow it, and the instruction is escalated to the nominated officer
The branch should release half the payment as a compromise
The branch should tell the customer that Tom approved the release
bank.explanation: Making the payment without consent could be a principal offence for the bank and the people involved. Seniority does not create a defence. The instruction itself should be escalated.

bank.question: Barclays only reviewed its exposure to Fowler Oldfield through customers like Stunt & Co after learning of the FCA's decision to prosecute NatWest. What should a bank do when law enforcement shares information about a customer's counterparty?
options: Wait until charges are brought before reviewing
Promptly re-assess the affected relationships, consider whether internal reports or SARs are needed and document the review
Close every account linked to the counterparty without review
Tell the customer about the law enforcement information
bank.explanation: The FCA criticised Barclays for not acting promptly on law enforcement information. A risk-based review with documented decisions is expected. Blanket closures without thought and telling the customer are both poor responses.

bank.question: Which statement about the threshold amount in POCA s.339A is correct for a bank operating an account?
options: It is GBP 3,000 by default, can be raised by an officer, and does not remove the duty to report suspicion
It is GBP 10,000 and exempts banks from reporting suspicion on transactions below that amount, unless the customer is already under investigation
It applies only to cash withdrawals by the customer
It is set by OFSI each year
bank.explanation: Section 339A sets a default GBP 3,000 threshold for deposit-taking bodies operating accounts, which an officer may raise. It provides an exemption from the principal offences for those acts; s.330 reporting still applies.

bank.question: A Larkhill customer is designated at 10 am. At 11 am a standing order from her account to her landlord is due. What should the bank do?
options: Let the standing order run, because it was set up before the designation
Pay it, because rent is a basic need
Wait 24 hours for the FCDO to confirm the listing
Stop the payment and freeze the account, then report to OFSI; any payment needs a licence or valid exception
bank.explanation: The freeze applies immediately on designation. Basic needs payments may be licensed by OFSI, but the bank cannot assume a licence. Existing payment instructions do not override the prohibition.

bank.question: A designated person holds 30% of a company, and an unconnected investor holds 70%. There is no evidence the designated person controls the board or affairs. Which is the best view?
options: The company is automatically frozen because a designated person is a shareholder, whatever the size of the stake or the level of control
The company must be reported to the NCA as a SAR
Probably not met on these facts, but the bank should record its assessment and watch for changes
The bank must exit the company immediately
bank.explanation: OFSI's guidance uses more than 50%, majority board appointment rights, or control of affairs. A 30% holding without control does not meet the test, but OFSI advises staying vigilant in case the stake or control changes.

bank.question: A sanctions alert shows a partial name match with no date of birth on the incoming payment message. What is the appropriate action?
options: Release it, because partial matches are always false positives
Freeze it and report a confirmed breach to OFSI at once
Hold the payment and seek more identifying information before deciding, documenting the outcome
Return it to the sender with a note about sanctions
bank.explanation: A partial match without key identifiers needs investigation, not automatic release or an assumed breach. Returning funds could be a dealing if it is a true match.

bank.question: A designated person asks Larkhill to transfer frozen funds to pay a UK law firm. The law firm says the fees are reasonable. What must be in place before the bank pays?
options: A letter from the law firm confirming fees are reasonable
An OFSI licence covering the payment, with any conditions met
Approval from the FCA
Consent from the NCA under POCA
bank.explanation: OFSI's guidance says legal fees can be licensed, but the payment must be authorised by OFSI. The law firm's view, FCA approval or NCA consent cannot substitute for a sanctions licence.

bank.question: Starling's breach of its agreed requirement not to onboard high-risk customers involved more than 54,000 accounts. What wider lesson does this offer a bank's leadership?
options: Requirements agreed with the FCA are informal guidance that can be relaxed during periods of rapid growth, as long as the board is informed
Agreed regulatory restrictions must be built into onboarding systems and monitored, or growth will override them
Restrictions apply only to the compliance team, not front-line onboarding
Breaching a requirement is acceptable if the accounts are later closed
bank.explanation: Starling opened over 54,000 accounts for about 49,000 high-risk customers in breach of the requirement. Controls must be engineered into processes and monitored, especially during fast growth.

bank.question: Which statement correctly describes how proliferation financing is built into the MLRs?
options: PF is covered only by sanctions law and not by the MLRs
PF controls apply only to firms that finance arms exporters
Banks must assess PF risk (reg 18A), manage it with policies and controls (reg 19A), and include PF in regulation 24 training
PF was added to the MLRs by SI 2026/621 in June 2026
bank.explanation: Regulations 18A and 19A require PF risk assessment and controls, and regulation 24 was amended from 1 September 2022 to cover PF. Sanctions screening complements these duties.

bank.question: A trade customer's letter of credit for electronic components is routed via a freight forwarder that recently changed its name and address. No party is designated. What is the most useful next step?
options: Issue the letter of credit, because screening is clear
Ask for end-user and export licence details, check the forwarder's history and ownership, and escalate if concerns remain
Report the customer to OFSI straight away as a confirmed sanctions breach, and freeze all of its accounts until OFSI replies
Refuse and tell the customer the bank suspects proliferation
bank.explanation: Name and address changes by intermediaries and unclear end use are classic PF warning signs. Gathering facts and escalating fits regs 18A and 19A. Screening clear does not mean low risk, and telling the customer of the suspicion risks tipping off.

bank.question: Larkhill discovers that, for six months, a data feed error meant new additions to the UK Sanctions List were not loaded into its screening tool. What should it do?
options: Fix the feed, re-screen the period, and report any breaches or suspected matches to OFSI promptly
Fix the feed quietly, screen only future activity, and mention the incident in the next annual frozen assets review rather than reporting it now
Report the matter to the NCA as a SAR only
Wait for the annual frozen assets review to report
bank.explanation: Like Starling, the bank must find out what it missed. Look-back screening and prompt OFSI reporting of breaches or suspected designated persons are needed; OFSI considers prompt self-disclosure when deciding how to respond.

bank.question: Who must tell OFSI as soon as practicable when, in the course of business, they know or reasonably suspect that a person is designated or that a breach has occurred?
options: Relevant firms such as banks, including individuals working for them
Only the bank's nominated officer
Only the FCA
Only firms that hold frozen assets
bank.explanation: OFSI's guidance says the reporting obligation applies to relevant firms, including individuals working for them, where the information arises in the course of business.

bank.question: Larkhill's training records show who completed the AML module but not what it covered. Under regulation 24(1)(b), what is the weakness?
options: There is no weakness, because attendance is all that matters
Training records only need to be kept for agents, because employees' training is already evidenced by their signed employment contracts
Training records must be sent to the NCA each year
A written record of the measures and training given is required, so content as well as attendance should be evidenced
bank.explanation: Regulation 24(1)(b) requires a written record of the measures taken and the training given. Showing what was taught, and to whom, is how the bank evidences that training matches roles and risks.

bank.question: Which statement about agents and regulation 24 is correct?
options: Agents are never covered because they are not employees, so the bank only needs to check that their own employer trains them
Agents are covered only if they handle cash
Since January 2020, agents doing relevant work must also be made aware of the law and trained regularly
Agents are covered only from 30 June 2026
bank.explanation: SI 2019/1511 added agents doing comparable work to regulation 24 from 10 January 2020. The test is the nature of their work, not whether they handle cash.

bank.question: A senior manager says: 'I approved the AML policy, so I've done my part.' Which response is most accurate?
options: Correct: approval is the senior manager's only duty
Senior managers have no AML duties under the MLRs or the SM&CR; only the MLRO can be held responsible for weaknesses in the controls
Approval is required, but the senior manager must also make sure policies are reviewed, resourced and working
Only the board as a whole can be held responsible
bank.explanation: Regulation 19 requires senior management approval and regular review. Under the SM&CR, a responsible senior manager is expected to take reasonable steps to make sure controls work, and the FCA can pursue officers knowingly concerned in breaches.

bank.question: A business relationship had a transaction 12 years before it ended. Under regulation 40, how long must the bank keep that transaction record after the relationship ends?
options: It need not keep transaction records within a relationship for more than ten years
Five years from the end of the relationship, with no upper limit
Indefinitely, because old transactions are high risk
Only until the account is closed
bank.explanation: Regulation 40(3) sets five years from the end of the relationship, but regulation 40(4) caps the retention of transaction records within a relationship at ten years. Personal data must then be deleted unless an exception applies.

bank.question: Under regulation 21, screening of relevant employees must assess which two things?
options: Their credit score and criminal record only
Their academic qualifications and years of service
Their sales performance and customer feedback
Their skills, knowledge and expertise to do the job, and their conduct and integrity
bank.explanation: Regulation 21(2)(a) defines screening as assessing skills, knowledge and expertise, and conduct and integrity, both before appointment and during it.

bank.question: An FCA investigation finds Larkhill breached the MLRs, but the bank shows it took all reasonable steps and exercised all due diligence. What follows under regulation 76?
options: The FCA must impose a reduced penalty
The FCA must not impose a penalty for that contravention
The FCA may still impose any penalty it chooses
The case must be passed to OFSI
bank.explanation: Regulation 76(4) prevents a penalty where the firm took all reasonable steps and exercised all due diligence. The burden in practice falls on the firm to evidence those steps, which is why records matter.

bank.question: When deciding whether a bank breached the MLRs, what must the FCA or a court consider about guidance?
options: Only guidance published by FATF
Whether the bank followed relevant guidance issued by the FCA or by another body and approved by the Treasury
Nothing: guidance has no legal effect, so the FCA and courts look only at the wording of the Regulations themselves
Only guidance the bank wrote for itself
bank.explanation: Regulations 76(6) and 86(2) require consideration of whether the firm followed relevant guidance issued by the FCA or approved by HM Treasury. Following such guidance helps a firm show it complied.

bank.question: HSBC's monitoring weaknesses lasted from 2010 to 2018, despite being highlighted on numerous occasions. Which governance lesson is most relevant to a responsible senior manager?
options: Automated monitoring removes the need for senior oversight
Known weaknesses need owned, funded and tracked remediation, with independent testing that fixes work
Remediation can be paused once the FCA has been told
Monitoring scenarios should never be changed once approved
bank.explanation: The FCA noted that HSBC's systems were ineffective for a long period despite repeated warnings. Senior managers must make sure problems are fixed in good time and tested, not just reported.

bank.question: Which pair of roles must Larkhill identify to the FCA within 14 days of appointment under regulation 21(4)?
options: The officer responsible for MLR compliance and the nominated officer
The chief executive and the chief financial officer
The head of internal audit and the data protection officer
The sanctions officer and the head of fraud
bank.explanation: Regulation 21(4) requires notification of the board member or senior manager responsible for compliance (reg 21(1)(a)) and the nominated officer (reg 21(3)), and any later appointments to either role.
